guanju.summary: The opening poem of the Zhounan group, in the 'Airs' division. Starting from the matching cries of ospreys, it follows a gentleman who longs for a lovely girl, cannot win her and lies awake, until he welcomes her with zithers, lutes, bells and drums. Moving from evocation into plain statement, it is the best-known courtship poem in the Book of Songs (Shijing) and stands first in the whole book.
guanju.translation:
Guan-guan cry the ospreys, on the islet in the river.
A gentle, lovely girl - a fine match for the noble man.
The water-mallow grows uneven; left and right we gather it as it drifts.
A gentle, lovely girl - awake and asleep he seeks her.
He seeks her and cannot find her; awake and asleep he pines for her.
Long, how long the night; he tosses and turns.
The water-mallow grows uneven; left and right we pick it.
A gentle, lovely girl - with zither and lute he befriends her.
The water-mallow grows uneven; left and right we choose it.
A gentle, lovely girl - with bells and drums he delights her.

glossary.en: guan guan - the cry of a bird
glossary.note: Sound-word for the answering calls of a male and female osprey.

glossary.en: ju jiu - osprey, a water bird
glossary.note: A waterbird said to be faithful to its mate; another view makes it a fish-eating raptor.
Quiet, graceful and fair.
A spouse; hao qiu is a good match.
A water plant with floating leaves and edible tender stems and leaves; the poem uses it to open the song.
Wu is waking and mei is sleeping; together they mean day and night.

glossary.en: mao - to pick out, to choose
glossary.note: To select; one view takes it as 'to boil'.
Used here as a verb: to draw close and be friendly.

guanju.background: The Mao Preface (Mao Shi Xu) takes this as praise of the virtue of a queen, the 'beginning of the Airs', used to teach proper married life. Zhu Xi (1130-1200) of the Song dynasty (960-1279), in his Collected Commentary on the Songs, thought it was about King Wen of the Zhou dynasty (c. 1046-256 BC) and his wife Taisi. Today it is mostly read as a courtship poem following a man's heart from wooing to marriage, and some think it was sung at a wedding.

getan.summary: The second poem of the Zhounan, in the Airs. It is mostly plain description. The first two stanzas show kudzu growing and then being cut, boiled and woven into cloth; the last shows a young woman preparing to visit her parents, washing her clothes and telling her governess. The mood is light, showing the work and filial feeling of women of old.
getan.translation:
The kudzu vine spreads and spreads, creeping across the middle of the valley;
its leaves are lush and green.
The yellow birds fly about,
and settle on the bushes,
their song so clear.
The kudzu vine spreads and spreads, creeping across the middle of the valley;
its leaves are thick and dense.
We cut it and we boil it,
we make fine cloth and coarse;
wearing it, I never tire of it.
I tell my governess,
I tell her I am going home.
First I will clean my everyday clothes,
first I will rinse my robes.
Which need washing and which do not?
I am going home to ask after my parents.

glossary.note: To lengthen, to creep.
To spread and extend.

glossary.en: chi, xi - fine and coarse kudzu cloth
glossary.note: Chi is fine kudzu cloth; xi is the coarse kind.
To be weary of or to dislike.
A woman teacher who trained young women.

glossary.en: bo - a particle meaning 'first, for now'
glossary.note: A helping word with the sense of 'for the moment'.

glossary.en: wu, huan - to clean, to rinse
glossary.note: Wu is to remove dirt from clothes (one view says it means underclothes); huan is to wash (outer robes).

glossary.en: gui ning - to visit one's parents after marriage
glossary.note: When a married woman returns home to see her parents.

getan.background: The Mao Preface reads this as showing a queen who worked hard at women's tasks while still in her parents' home and never forgot her origins; Zhu Xi thought the queen herself was speaking. Today it is mostly read as a song of a noblewoman about to visit her parents, moving from the growth of the kudzu and the weaving to the washing and the homecoming. Its tone is plain, and it is material for the study of Zhou weaving and women's lives.

juaner.summary: A poem of the Zhounan, in the Airs. A woman picks cocklebur but cannot fill her basket, lost in thoughts of the one far away. The last three stanzas turn to imagine him climbing hills, his horse worn out and his servant sick, and drowning his sorrow in wine; she goes from herself to him and describes longing through the imagined scene, a distinctive structure.
juaner.translation:
I pick and pick the cocklebur, yet cannot fill my shallow basket.
Alas, I long for my man, and set it down on the great road.
I climb that rocky height; my horse is worn out.
Let me pour from that bronze flagon, so as not to brood for ever.
I climb that high ridge; my horse's coat has gone dark and yellow.
Let me pour from that rhino-horn cup, so as not to grieve for ever.
I climb that earth-topped rocky hill; my horse is broken down.
My groom is sick;
oh, what a sigh!

glossary.note: A wild plant whose young leaves can be eaten.
To place or lay.
A broad highway.
An earthen hill with stones; another view says a steep, high mountain.

glossary.en: hui tui - worn out (pronounced hui tui)
glossary.note: The look of a horse that is tired and sick.

glossary.en: jin lei - a bronze wine vessel (pronounced lei)
glossary.note: A wine vessel made of metal.
A wine cup made from rhinoceros horn.

glossary.en: ju - a rocky hill topped with earth (pronounced ju)
glossary.note: A stony hill covered with soil.

juaner.background: The Mao Preface takes this as a poem of a queen helping her lord and thinking of worthy ministers; Zhu Xi read it as a queen thinking of King Wen away at war. Later readers mostly take it as a wife's poem of longing, and some think the last three stanzas are the voice of a soldier homesick on the march. Because the speaker changes without warning, readings have always differed. It is a famous example of describing the other person's side to show one's own feeling.

jiumu.summary: A poem of the Zhounan, in the Airs, three stanzas with only the verbs changed. The kudzu clinging to the drooping tree opens the song, and each stanza wishes the noble man steady good fortune. The repetition deepens the meaning at each turn. It is a short song of blessing for a noble.
jiumu.translation:
In the south stands a drooping tree, with kudzu vines clinging to it.
Happy is the noble man; may blessings bring him peace.
In the south stands a drooping tree, with kudzu vines covering it.
Happy is the noble man; may blessings support him.
In the south stands a drooping tree, with kudzu vines winding round it.
Happy is the noble man; may blessings complete him.

glossary.note: A tree whose branches bend downward (jiu).
A creeping plant of the kudzu kind.
To twine and climb.
A particle that ends the line.
Blessings and rank. Lu stands for 'rank, salary'; another view takes it as 'the good fortune one steps into'.

glossary.en: sui - to settle, to bring peace
glossary.note: To make steady and well.

glossary.en: huang, ying - to cover, to wind round
glossary.note: Huang is to cover over; ying is to encircle.
To help and prop up.

jiumu.background: The Mao Preface says it shows a queen who is generous to those below her, so that the concubines feel no jealousy and are loyal; Zhu Xi thought it was the concubines wishing the queen well. Today it is mostly taken as a song of blessing for a newly married couple or for a noble. Opening with an evocative image and changing a word in each stanza is typical of the way the Book of Songs repeats its stanzas and lines.

zhongsi.summary: A poem of the Zhounan, in the Airs. The grasshoppers swarming and humming stand for a large family, and it is a song wishing people many sons and grandsons. Its three stanzas repeat with changed adjectives in a lively rhythm, using both comparison and evocation.
zhongsi.translation:
The grasshopper's wings, shen shen, so many!
May it be right for your sons and grandsons, zhen zhen, thriving!
The grasshopper's wings, hong hong, humming!
May it be right for your sons and grandsons, sheng sheng, going on and on!
The grasshopper's wings, yi yi, gathered together!
May it be right for your sons and grandsons, zhe zhe, in harmony!

glossary.note: An insect of the locust and grasshopper kind, said to lay many eggs at a time.
The look of great numbers.
A word of blessing; another view says 'ought to'.
Flourishing and generous.

glossary.en: hong hong - the sound of a swarm (pronounced hong)
glossary.note: The buzzing of a swarm of insects in flight.
Continuing without end.
The look of things assembled together.

glossary.en: zhe zhe - many and in harmony
glossary.note: Numerous and gathered peacefully.

zhongsi.background: The Mao Preface says it praises a queen who is not jealous, and so has many descendants; Zhu Xi took it as the concubines praising the queen by the grasshopper. Today most readers see it as a song for a wedding or for wishing a family many descendants. 'Zhong si' later became a stock allusion for wishing someone many sons.

taoyao.summary: A famous poem of the Zhounan, in the Airs, congratulating a young woman on her marriage. Blossoming peach, then fruit, then thick leaves stand for the bride's youth and beauty and the thriving of the new household, in a mix of evocation and comparison. The language is bright and the images vivid.

glossary.note: Luxuriant and delicate.
Bright as fire when in flower.
Another way of writing 'flower'.
'This person', meaning the bride.

glossary.en: yu gui - to go to one's new home
glossary.note: Yu is a particle; in old usage a woman's marriage was called 'returning' (gui).
To be gentle and treat kindly.
Describes large, full fruit.
Thick and flourishing plants.

taoyao.background: The Mao Preface says it shows a queen's influence at work, so that marriages came at the right time; Zhu Xi likewise took it as praise of a bride. Readers today agree it is a wedding song. 'Tao yao' and 'zhuo zhuo qi hua' later became standard phrases for a new marriage and for a woman's beauty.

fuyi.summary: A poem of the Zhounan, in the Airs, about women picking plantain together. Only the verb changes, from picking to tucking the fruit into the belt, each stanza more exact than the last. The rhythm is quick, like a work song, a typical folk ballad.
fuyi.translation:
We pick and pick the plantain; let us pick it.
We pick and pick the plantain; let us have it.
We pick and pick the plantain; let us gather it up.
We pick and pick the plantain; let us strip it off the stalk.
We pick and pick the plantain; let us carry it in our skirts.
We pick and pick the plantain; let us tuck our skirts in our belts to hold it.

glossary.note: Common plantain; its seeds and whole plant are used as medicine, and old people thought it helped with having children.

glossary.en: bo yan - a helping phrase meaning 'let us'
glossary.note: Bo carries the sense 'for the moment' and yan is a particle.
To obtain.
To gather.
To strip along the stalk with the hand.

glossary.en: jie - to carry in a held-up skirt (pronounced jie)
glossary.note: To hold up the hem of the robe with the hand and fill it.

glossary.en: xie - to tuck the hem into the belt (pronounced xie)
glossary.note: To tuck the skirt hem into the belt to make a pouch.

fuyi.background: The Mao Preface says it is about peace in the land, with women glad to have children; Zhu Xi said it was women singing as they picked plantain in the fields. Tradition links plantain with helping conception. Today it is often read as a pure work song, whose poetry lies in the rhythm of the actions and the happy mood.

hanguang.summary: A poem of the Zhounan, in the Airs: a woodcutter admires a girl wandering by the Han River but knows he cannot win her. The breadth of the Han and the length of the Yangtze stand for what can be seen but not reached. Three stanzas repeat the refrain, with a gentle, restrained sadness.

glossary.note: A big, tall tree.
Xiu is to rest; xi is a helping particle like si. The si in 'qiu si', 'yong si' and 'fang si' in the poem is also only a particle.
A woman out walking; one view takes her as the goddess of the Han.
Long.

glossary.en: fang - to cross on a raft (used as a verb)
glossary.note: Here it is a verb: to cross water on a raft of wood.

glossary.en: qiao qiao cuo xin - tall, tangled brushwood
glossary.note: Qiao qiao means standing out above the rest; cuo xin is a jumble of firewood.
Chu is a thorny shrub; lou is a wild plant of the artemisia kind, used as fuel.
To feed horses.

hanguang.background: The Mao Preface says it shows virtue spreading far, so that King Wen's teaching made men and women respectful and unapproachable. Zhu Xi said it describes the custom of the Yangtze and Han region, where women had been taught to be chaste and men admired them in vain. Today it is mostly read as a love song of unrequited longing and is one of the sources of the theme of love seen but not reached.

quechao.summary: A poem of the Shaonan, in the Airs, a song for escorting or welcoming a bride. The dove living in the magpie's nest opens it, and three stanzas show a hundred carriages meeting and sending the bride, with the verbs 'meet, escort, complete' building up the grandness of the wedding.

glossary.en: wei - a particle at the start of a line
glossary.note: A helping word used at the start of a clause.
The cuckoo-like dove (shi jiu), which does not build a nest and often borrows a magpie's.

glossary.en: zhi zi yu gui - this girl goes to her new home
glossary.note: The girl is marrying.
Liang is the same as 'chariot'; a hundred means a large wedding party.
To welcome.
To occupy.
To send off.
Full; meaning many attendants and the dowry party.

quechao.background: The Mao Preface says it praises the virtue of the wife of a lord, the dove in the magpie's nest standing for her taking charge of her husband's house; Zhu Xi took it to show the ladies of the southern states being taught by King Wen. Today it is mostly read as a noble wedding song. The saying 'the dove takes the magpie's nest' first meant a bride moving into her husband's house, and only later gained a bad sense.

caifan.summary: A poem of the Shaonan, in the Airs, about women gathering white mugwort for a lord's sacrifice. Three stanzas, the first two as question and answer on where it is picked and what it is for; the last shows her working day and night for the court and going home in full headdress. It reflects the sacrifices of the time and the labour of serving nobles.
caifan.translation:
Where do we pick the white mugwort? By the pond, on the islet.
Where is it used? In the lord's rites.
Where do we pick the white mugwort? In the mountain stream.
Where is it used? In the lord's palace.
Her headdress rises high; morning and night she serves at the court.
Her headdress sways slowly; then she goes back home.

glossary.note: Used in ancient sacrifices as a mat for the offerings or for steaming.
Zhao is a pond; zhi is a small islet in the water.

glossary.en: gong hou zhi shi - the lord's affairs
glossary.note: That is, the sacrifices.
A form of a word for the false hair worn by married women.

glossary.en: tong tong - lofty headdress, or reverent
glossary.note: Describes the headdress piled high or a respectful manner; views differ.

glossary.en: su ye zai gong - at the court morning and night
glossary.note: Serving in the lord's house early and late.
Unhurried.
A particle.

caifan.background: The Mao Preface says it praises a lady for taking part in sacrifices and never failing in her duty; Zhu Xi held a similar view, taking it as a lord's wife of the southern states gathering the mugwort herself. Some modern readers instead see it as a song of women (even palace servants) working for nobles. Mugwort was a common item in sacrifice, so the poem gives details of Zhou rites.

caochong.summary: A poem of the Shaonan, in the Airs, of a wife in autumn who sees insects leaping and picks bracken and vetch while she thinks of her husband far away, imagining the joy of meeting. Three stanzas set 'not yet seen' against 'once seen', with feeling moving from anxiety to peace, both plain statement and evocation.
caochong.translation:
Yao-yao chirp the grass insects, ti-ti leap the grasshoppers.
I have not yet seen my lord; my heart is heavy with worry.
Once I have seen him, once I have met him, my heart will settle.
I climb that southern hill, and pick the bracken.
I have not yet seen my lord; my heart aches with anxiety.
Once I have seen him, once I have met him, my heart will be glad.
I climb that southern hill, and pick the vetch.
I have not yet seen my lord; my heart is sad and grieved.
Once I have seen him, once I have met him, my heart will be at ease.

glossary.en: yao yao - the chirp of insects (pronounced yao)
glossary.note: The sound of insects.
The look of jumping.

glossary.en: fu zhong - a kind of grasshopper
glossary.note: A grasshopper-like insect. The Mao commentary calls it the male of the grass insect; in the Songs, grass insects and grasshoppers are used to suggest a couple together.
A helping word.
To come together.
To set down; the worried heart set down means peace of mind.
Two wild greens whose young leaves can be eaten.
Troubled and uneasy.

caochong.background: The Mao Preface says it shows the wife of a grandee guarding herself by ritual; Zhu Xi thought it was written by the wife of an official away on service, longing for him. Modern readers mostly take it as a poem of a woman missing someone. The phrase 'once seen' is read by some as 'having seen him', by others as 'if I should see him', so the whole may be taken as imagining while she longs.

caiping.summary: A poem of the Shaonan, in the Airs, following a young woman through the whole preparation of a sacrifice: gathering duckweed and pondweed, boiling them and setting out the offering. It is all question and answer, orderly and grave, and shows how Zhou women took part in the rites of the family temple.
caiping.translation:
Where do we pick the duckweed? By the southern stream.
Where do we pick the pondweed? In that roadside runoff.
What do we hold it in? Baskets, square and round.
What do we boil it in? Tripods and cauldrons.
Where do we set it out? Under the window of the ancestral hall.
Who presides over it? A reverent young girl.

glossary.en: ping - duckweed or four-leaf water fern
glossary.note: A water fern, a vegetable used in sacrifice.
A water plant offered with the ping in sacrifice.
Ditches that hold water by the road.
To cook.

glossary.en: qi, fu - a tripod pot, a cauldron
glossary.note: Qi is a pot with three legs; fu is a pot without legs.
To lay out the offerings.
To lead the sacrifice; one view says it means the person who stands for the ancestor to receive the offering.
A young woman; ji means the youngest in the order of birth.

caiping.background: The Mao Preface says it is about a grandee's wife who obeys the rules and leads the sacrifice; Zhu Xi also took it as the wife of an official making the offering. Another view makes it a 'sacrifice of completed training' that a girl made to her ancestors in the temple before marriage. Either way, the poem's stress is on reverence and thrift in preparing the sacrifice.

gantang.summary: A poem of the Shaonan, in the Airs, a short song in which the people remember Lord Shao. They show their memory by not cutting or felling the sweet pear tree. In three stanzas the 'do not cut', 'do not harm' and 'do not bend' grow in force; the feeling is sincere and the language plain.
gantang.translation:
Thick and shady stands the sweet pear; do not cut it, do not fell it - it is where Lord Shao camped.
Thick and shady stands the sweet pear; do not cut it, do not harm it - it is where Lord Shao rested.
Thick and shady stands the sweet pear; do not cut it, do not bend it - it is where Lord Shao paused.

glossary.en: bi fei - thick and shady (pronounced bi fei)
glossary.note: Describes a tree with small, dense leaves.
A wild pear tree whose fruit can be eaten.
To cut down.
Usually taken as Duke Shao (Shi) at the start of the Zhou; another view says Duke Mu of Shao in the time of King Xuan.
To make a shelter in the grass and live there.
A variant of the word for resting.
The Mao commentary says it means 'to pull out'.
To halt for the night.

gantang.background: According to the Mao commentary and the Records of the Grand Historian, Lord Shao used to hear cases and handle affairs under a sweet pear tree, and the people, grateful for his rule, made this song. Later people used 'the sweet pear's lasting love' to praise officials. Most today accept this account, although opinions still differ on who Lord Shao was.

xinglu.summary: A poem of the Shaonan, in the Airs, in which a woman firmly refuses a forced marriage. Dew on the road, the sparrow pecking and the rat gnawing open the poem, and her tone is hard as she answers the threat of a lawsuit. It is a work of independence and constancy by a woman of old.
xinglu.translation:
The dew on the road is damp and heavy.
Would I not go, early or late?
I say there is too much dew on the road.
Who says the sparrow has no horn?
How else would it pierce my roof?
Who says you have no wife?
Why else do you bring me before the court?
Though you bring me before the court,
our match still lacks what it needs.
Who says the rat has no teeth?
How else would it bore through my wall?
Who says you have no wife?
Why else do you bring me to law?
Though you bring me to law,
I will still not follow you.

glossary.note: Moist.

glossary.en: xing lu - dew on the road
glossary.note: Dew on the road.
To call down, to cause.
Yu is a criminal case; song is a civil dispute, so here, going to court.

glossary.en: shi jia bu zu - the marriage is not complete
glossary.note: The betrothal gifts are lacking, or the wedding does not follow the rites.
A wall.
The same word as 'you'.
The ancients thought a sparrow had a horn to peck through a roof and a rat teeth to gnaw through a wall; her rhetorical question mocks the man's forced argument.

xinglu.background: The Mao Preface says Lord Shao heard a case where a woman refused a violent man; Zhu Xi took the poem as a chaste girl's refusal of an assault. The line about 'who says you have no home' is read two ways: 'who says you have no wife' and 'who says a woman has no way to marry properly'. Today it is mostly read as a poem of refusing a marriage.

yeyousijun.summary: A poem of the Shaonan, in the Airs, in which a hunter offers game to win a girl whose heart has stirred with spring, and she shyly tells him not to be rash. The language is lively, with a strong flavour of the life of ordinary people, in plain statement together with evocation.
yeyousijun.translation:
In the wilds lies a dead roe deer; we wrap it in white rushes.
A girl is stirred by spring; a fine young man woos her.
In the wood there are oak shrubs; in the wilds lies a dead deer,
bound up in white rushes; there is a girl like jade.
Slowly, gently, now,
do not tug at my kerchief,
do not set the shaggy dog barking.

glossary.note: A small deer.
Thatch grass, often used to wrap gifts.
Awakened to love.
A flattering term for a man.
To wrap and tie.

glossary.en: shu er tuo tuo - slow and calm
glossary.note: Gentle and unhurried; tuo tuo is the look of slowness.
A cloth worn at a woman's belt.
A long-haired dog.

yeyousijun.background: The Mao Preface says it describes a time of chaos and violence in which women still kept to ritual and were not defiled; Zhu Xi regarded it as a poem of licentious elopement. Today it is mostly seen as a simple folk courtship poem showing the shyness and charm of a rendezvous.

baizhou.summary: A poem of the Bei Airs: a person in a hard place, harmed by petty men and unable to rely on brothers, is full of anger and grief with no way out, and can only watch sun and moon take turns and sigh. It opens with a cypress boat adrift, mixing plain statement with comparison, and is a famous poem of sorrow in the Book of Songs.
baizhou.translation:
A cypress boat drifts, drifting on the current.
Restless, I cannot sleep, as if with a hidden grief.
It is not that I have no wine, with which to wander and amuse myself.
My heart is not a mirror, to take in everything.
I have brothers too, but I cannot lean on them.
I went to tell them my trouble, and met their anger.
My heart is not a stone, to be rolled about.
My heart is not a mat, to be rolled up.
My bearing is dignified and graceful; there is nothing in it to pick out as fault.
My heart is troubled and sore, resentful at the pack of petty men.
I have met many troubles and endured no little insult.
Quietly I think it over, wake, and beat my breast.
O sun, O moon, why do you take turns and grow dim?
The grief in my heart is like an unwashed garment.
Quietly I think it over; I cannot spread my wings and fly!

glossary.note: The look of a heart that is uneasy.
'Not'.

glossary.en: yi ao yi you - to go out and amuse oneself
glossary.note: To go out and roam so as to ease one's grief.
A mirror reflects everything without picking and choosing; the speaker means that he cannot put up with everything alike.

glossary.en: wei yi di di - dignified and graceful
glossary.note: Solemn and refined in bearing.

glossary.en: gou min - to meet with trouble
glossary.note: To run into misfortune and worry.

glossary.en: wu pi you biao - to wake and beat the breast
glossary.note: Pi is to strike the breast; biao is the look of beating.

glossary.en: ri ju yue zhu - O sun, O moon
glossary.note: Ju and zhu are particles; the line is a cry to the sun and moon.

baizhou.background: The Mao Preface says it is about a humane person who cannot get on, and is pushed aside by petty men. Old accounts such as the Biographies of Women took it as a poem of a widow of Wei keeping faith; Zhu Xi thought it was written by a wife not favoured by her husband. Some modern readers take it as the self-account of a scholar out of favour, or a neglected woman. The line 「我心匪石，不可轉也」 ("my heart is not a stone, to be rolled about") became a famous expression of constancy.

yanyan.summary: A poem of the Bei Airs, a farewell. The swallows in flight open it, and then she watches far, tears like rain, standing a long time. It ends with praise of the one who leaves. Some call it the earliest of all farewell poems.

glossary.note: Not in line; describes wings that do not match.

glossary.en: xie zhi hang zhi - rising and dipping
glossary.note: Jie is to fly upward; hang is to fly downward.
To marry, or to go back home.

glossary.en: Zhong shi - the second sister, or Lady Zhong
glossary.note: A person second in birth order.
Reliable and true.
Sincere and profound.

glossary.en: xian jun zhi si - remembering the late lord
glossary.note: To think of the previous ruler.

glossary.en: gua ren - 'the man of few virtues'
glossary.note: How a lord of old referred to himself.

yanyan.background: The Mao Preface says Zhuang Jiang of Wei saw off a concubine (Dai Gui) who was returning home. Another account says Ding Jiang of Wei saw off her daughter-in-law, or that the ruler of Wei saw off his sister on her marriage. Because the closing words 'to encourage me' are the ruler's voice, no account is settled. Whichever it is, the feeling of parting is deeply moving, and later writers often use 'the swallows fly' and 'gaze after her, cannot see her' to describe farewell.

kaifeng.summary: A poem of the Bei Airs in which a son praises his mother's toil and blames himself for not repaying her. The warm south wind blowing on the jujube shoots stands for a mother's labour in raising children; the tone is deeply felt but restrained.

glossary.en: kai feng - the warm south wind
glossary.note: A mild, soft wind from the south.
The young buds of the thorny jujube, standing for small children.
Hard labour.

glossary.en: ji xin (firewood) - jujube branches grown for firewood
glossary.note: The jujube grown to branches big enough for fuel, standing for sons who have grown up.
Sensible and virtuous.
A good man, a man with prospects.
A cold spring; Jun was a place in Wei that had one.

glossary.en: xian huan - sweet and clear (pronounced xian huan)
glossary.note: The gentle, flowing song of the yellow bird.

kaifeng.background: The Mao Preface says licentious ways were widespread in Wei, and a mother of seven sons could not settle in her home, so the poem praises the seven sons for doing their filial duty. Zhu Xi said the mother could not rest and her sons blamed themselves. Later writers use 'warm wind' and 'cold spring' to speak of a dutiful son's longing for his mother.

jigu.summary: A poem of the Bei Airs of a soldier of Wei on a distant campaign, who is anxious he may not return and recalls the vow he made with his love, 「執子之手，與子偕老」 ("I will hold your hand and grow old with you"), and ends in sorrow that they cannot be together.
jigu.translation:
The drum beats, tang tang; we leap up to drill with arms.
Some dig earthworks in the capital and wall Cao; I alone march south.
I follow Sun Zizhong to make peace between Chen and Song,
but he will not let me go home, and my heart is uneasy.
Where do we halt, where do we stay? Where have we lost our horses?
Where shall we look for them? Under the trees of the wood.
Death or life, parting or meeting, I made a vow with you:
I will hold your hand and grow old with you.
Alas, the parting is long, and I cannot live with you;
alas, the distance is far, and I cannot keep my word.

glossary.en: tang - sound of a drum (pronounced tang)
glossary.note: The beat of a drum.
To drill with arms, or to fight.

glossary.en: tu guo cheng Cao - earthworks in the capital, walls at Cao
glossary.note: Tu is building in earth, and Cao was a town of Wei; one set of men was building in the capital and another walling Cao.
Name of the general; one view says Gongsun Wenzhong.

glossary.en: bu wo yi gui - will not let me go home
glossary.note: He does not allow me to return.

glossary.en: yuan ju yuan chu - where to halt and stay
glossary.note: Where shall we stop and dwell?

glossary.en: qi kuo - parting and meeting (here, parting)
glossary.note: Meeting and parting, in this poem stressing parting.

glossary.en: cheng shuo - to make a vow
glossary.note: To swear an oath or agree on a promise.

jigu.background: The Mao Preface says it is a poem of grievance by the people of Wei against Zhouxu's cruel use of arms. Modern readers mostly take it as a song of grievance by a Wei soldier. The line 「執子之手，與子偕老」 was a vow made on the battlefield and only later became a common wedding blessing, a shift in meaning.

gufeng.summary: A poem of the Bei Airs in the voice of a wife cast off by her husband. She recalls hardships shared and her thrifty running of the home, and now that he has a new love he treats her as an enemy. Her sorrow is restrained. It is the source of the Chinese poems of the abandoned wife.
gufeng.translation:
Soft blows the valley wind, bringing cloud and rain.
We should strive with one heart, and not be angry.
When you pick turnip and radish, do you throw away the roots?
Do not betray the fair words; I would die with you.
I walk the road slowly, my heart unwilling.
It is not far, only near; you just see me to the threshold.
Who says sow-thistle is bitter? It is sweet as shepherd's purse.
You feast with your new bride, close as brother and brother.
The Jing is muddied by the Wei, yet its shallows stay clear.
You feast with your new bride, and will not bother with me.
Do not go to my weir, do not open my fish-trap.
I am not even accepted myself; how can I care what comes after me?
Where the water was deep, I crossed it by raft or by boat.
Where it was shallow, I waded or swam.
What we had or lacked, I strove to supply.
When neighbours had a death, I crawled to help.
You cannot cherish me, but treat me as an enemy.
You block my goodness, as if it were an unsold ware.
In the old days of fear and want I fell with you.
Now that we have life and means, you liken me to poison.
I laid in good store to meet the winter.
You feast with your new bride, using me to fend off poverty.
You rage and storm, and leave me the toil.
You do not think of the old days, when you came to me for rest.

glossary.note: To make a great effort.
Root vegetables whose roots and leaves are both eaten.
Kind words, meaning the vows made at the start.

glossary.en: yan er xin hun - you feast with your new wife
glossary.note: Yan is to be happy and at ease; hun is the same as 'marriage'.

glossary.en: Jing yi Wei zhuo - the Jing muddied by the Wei
glossary.note: The ancients thought the Jing was clear and the Wei muddy; the poem uses this to contrast new and old, though readings differ.
A weir is a dam to trap fish; a gou is a bamboo trap; both stand for a woman's home.
Good food laid up, such as pickled vegetables.

gufeng.background: The Mao Preface says it criticises husbands and wives who lost the proper way, so that a husband abandoned his old wife for a new marriage; Zhu Xi also took it as the words of a cast-off wife. Modern readers all take it as a poem of an abandoned wife; paired with 'A Man' in the Wei Airs, it is seen as the start of the abandoned-wife theme in Chinese literature.

shiwei.summary: A poem of the Bei Airs, a complaint of a labourer working in the evening dew who cannot go home. Its two stanzas repeat, opening with the question 'why not go home?'; the grievance is plain and strong without open anger.
shiwei.translation:
Dusk falls, dusk falls - why not go home?
If not for you, my lord, why be here in the dew?
Dusk falls, dusk falls - why not go home?
If not for your person, why be here in the mud?

glossary.note: Shi is a particle; wei is dim. So the sky is growing dark.
Why.

glossary.en: wei jun zhi gu - if not for you
glossary.note: Wei means 'if it were not'; jun is the lord or master.
In the midst of the dew.
The body, oneself.
In the mire.

shiwei.background: The Mao Preface says the Marquis of Li fled and lived in Wei, and his ministers urged him to go back. Zhu Xi did not adopt this account but guessed it was a poem urging the Marquis of Li to return. Today it is mostly read as a labourer's complaint, simple in words but with deep unease. Later 'shi wei' often means decline, or urging someone to retire.

beimen.summary: A poem of the Bei Airs about a minor official overloaded with duties and in poverty, whom his family also blame, and who can only sigh that Heaven has done it. The three stanzas repeat and the feeling deepens; it is a poem of complaint and satire.
beimen.translation:
I go out by the north gate, my heart heavy with grief.
Poor and in want, no one knows my hardship.
Enough! Heaven has done this; what is there to say?
The king's business is thrown to me, and every government task is piled on me.
When I come in from outside, my household blames me, one after another.
Enough! Heaven has done this; what is there to say?
The king's business presses on me; every government task is left to me.
When I come in from outside, my household taunts me by turns.
Enough! Heaven has done this; what is there to say?

glossary.note: Deeply sad.

glossary.en: zhong ju qie pin - poor and in want
glossary.note: Ju is being too poor to carry out the proper rites; zhong means 'already'.
A sigh of resignation.
To cast on someone.

glossary.en: yi pi yi wo - all of it added to me
glossary.note: Every task is added to me; pi means to add.
The people of the home.

glossary.en: jiao bian - in turn, all round
glossary.note: Taking turns, every one of them.
The same as another word for 'blame'.

beimen.background: The Mao Preface says it criticises a time when an official could not get on; Zhu Xi called it the sigh of a loyal minister of Wei. Most today read it as the complaint of a poor minor official, a rare poem in the Book of Songs about the hardship of low-ranking officials.

jingnv.summary: A poem of the Bei Airs about a pair of lovers meeting: the girl hides so the young man scratches his head in worry, then gives him a red tube and a reed shoot that he treasures. The language is lively and humorous, in plain statement.
jingnv.translation:
The quiet girl is lovely; she waits for me at the corner of the city wall.
She hides and I cannot see her; scratching my head, I pace to and fro.
The quiet girl is fair; she gives me a red tube.
The red tube glows; I love its beauty and yours.
From the pasture she brings a reed shoot, truly lovely and rare.
It is not that the shoot is lovely; it is a gift from a lovely one.

glossary.note: A calm and gentle girl; one view reads jing as 'good'.
Fair.

glossary.en: cheng yu - corner of the city wall
glossary.note: The corner of a wall.
A form of a word meaning 'conceal'.

glossary.en: chi chu - to pace, to hesitate
glossary.note: To walk back and forth unable to move forward.
Beautiful.
A red tube-shaped thing; one view says a red brush-handle, another a red plant.
The tender sprout of thatch grass, which the ancients gave as a token of parting or goodwill.

jingnv.background: The Mao Preface says it mocks the ruler of Wei for lacking the Way and his wife for lacking virtue; Zhu Xi took it as a poem of an illicit tryst. Modern readers agree it is a charming love song. The 'red tube' also later became a name for the pen of a court lady historian.

xiangshu.summary: A poem of the Yong Airs, a satire that scolds shameless people who ignore ritual. A rat has skin, teeth and limbs, so a man without these things is worse than a rat; three stanzas grow in force, in an angry tone with very sharp comparison.
xiangshu.translation:
Look at the rat - it has a skin; a man without dignity,
a man without dignity - why does he not die?
Look at the rat - it has teeth; a man without shame,
a man without shame - what is he waiting for, if not death?
Look at the rat - it has limbs; a man without ritual,
a man without ritual - why does he not hurry up and die?

glossary.en: xiang shu - look at the rat
glossary.note: Xiang is 'look at'; another view says Xiang Shu is a kind of rat.
Proper and grave bearing.
A borrowed form of 'shame'; another view says it means deportment.
To wait.
The limbs and body.
Swiftly.

xiangshu.background: The Mao Preface says it mocks those in power under Duke Wen of Wei for lacking ritual; Zhu Xi said it condemns people without ritual and rightness. Most today see it as a song of the people scolding nobles. Its words are fierce and rare in the Book of Songs.

zaichi.summary: A poem of the Yong Airs. Tradition says it was written by the Lady of Xu, who heard that the Di tribes had destroyed her native state of Wei and wished to go home to console its ruler, but was stopped by the grandees of Xu. She tells of her rush to Wei, scolds the Xu grandees for their short sight, and says she wants to seek help from a great state. The feeling is intense, and it is one of the few poems in the Book of Songs with a named author.
zaichi.translation:
Gallop on, drive on, to go home and comfort the Marquis of Wei.
Far the horses drive, until we reach Cao.
A grandee has come trudging over hills and streams, and my heart is troubled.
Since you do not approve of me, I cannot turn back;
I see you mean no good, and my thoughts of home do not grow distant.
Since you do not approve of me, I cannot turn and cross back;
I see you mean no good, and my thoughts are not shut away.
I climb that high ridge and pick the fritillary.
A woman is full of feeling, yet each has her own way.
The people of Xu blame me - they are childish and foolish.
I walk through the fields, where the wheat grows thick;
I will appeal to a great state - on whom shall I rely, who will come?
You grandees and gentlemen, do not find fault with me;
all your hundred plans are worse than where I am going.

glossary.en: zai - a particle meaning 'then, and so'
glossary.note: A helping word with the sense of 'thereupon'.
To offer condolences to someone whose state has fallen or whose ruler has died.

glossary.en: Cao - Cao, a town of Wei
glossary.note: After Wei was destroyed, Duke Dai stayed there for a time.

glossary.en: ba she - to trudge over hill and stream
glossary.note: To cross hills and rivers on a long road.
To agree with and praise.
Shut off; another view says careful, far-seeing.
A medicinal bulb that the ancients thought could cure melancholy.
To report to, here to ask a great state for help.

zaichi.background: The Mao Preface and the Zuo Commentary both name the author as the Lady of Xu, a daughter of the ducal house of Wei who married the Duke of Xu. When she heard that the Di had broken Wei, she wanted to go home to mourn but could not. It is taken to be the earliest surviving poem in China with a woman's name attached. The line 「女子善懷，亦各有行」 ("a woman is full of feeling, yet each has her own way") shows a woman's self-awareness.

qiao.summary: A poem of the Wei Airs in praise of a gentleman. The green bamboo by the bend of the Qi opens it; the man's looks, dress and character are described, and 「如切如磋，如琢如磨」 ("as if cut, as if filed, as if carved, as if polished") is a figure for steady self-improvement. Three stanzas build in steps, mixing comparison and evocation.
qiao.translation:
I look at the bend of the Qi, where green bamboo grows lithe and lush.
There is a refined gentleman, as if cut and as if filed,
as if carved and as if polished;
solemn, imposing, shining, magnificent.
There is a refined gentleman, who can never be forgotten.
I look at the bend of the Qi, where green bamboo grows deep green.
There is a refined gentleman, his ear-pendants are shining gems,
the seams of his leather cap glitter like stars;
solemn, imposing, shining, magnificent.
There is a refined gentleman, who can never be forgotten.
I look at the bend of the Qi, where green bamboo grows thick as a mat.
There is a refined gentleman, like gold, like tin,
like a jade tablet, like a jade disc;
broad-minded and easy-going,
leaning on the carriage's double rail,
good at jesting,
and never harsh.

glossary.en: Qi ao - the bend of the Qi
glossary.note: The curved bank of the River Qi.
Soft, graceful and thick.
A form of a word meaning 'elegant, full of polish'.

glossary.en: ru qie ru cuo, ru zhuo ru mo - as if cut and filed, carved and polished
glossary.note: Working bone and horn, jade and stone; a figure for the need to keep improving in learning and character.

glossary.en: se, xian - solemn, imposing (xian pronounced xian)
glossary.note: Se is dignified; xian is stately and broad.
To forget.

glossary.en: chong er xiu ying - ear-pendants of bright gems
glossary.note: Jade ornaments hung beside the cap; xiu ying means gleaming fine jade.

glossary.en: kuai bian ru xing - the cap seams like stars
glossary.note: The seam of the leather cap is set with gems that sparkle like stars.

qiao.background: The Mao Preface says it praises the virtue of Duke Wu of Wei, and the Discourses of the States records that in old age he warned himself. The idea 'qie cuo zhuo mo' later became an idiom, and Zigong quotes this poem when discussing self-cultivation in the Analects. Today it is mostly read as praise of a noble gentleman.

shuoren.summary: A poem of the Wei Airs praising Zhuang Jiang, wife of Duke Zhuang of Wei. It gives her family, her looks, the carriages and escort of her wedding journey, the river and its fish, and the train of ladies who came with her. The lines starting 「手如柔荑」 ("her hands like soft reed shoots") are among the most famous descriptions of a woman's beauty in Chinese, a piece of plain description with many similes.
shuoren.translation:
The tall beauty is slender, in brocade with a plain coat over it.
Daughter of the Marquis of Qi, wife of the Marquis of Wei,
younger sister of the Crown Prince, sister-in-law of the Marquis of Xing,
and the Duke of Tan is her brother-in-law.
Her hands are like soft reed shoots, her skin like congealed fat,
her neck like a grub, her teeth like gourd seeds,
her brow like a cicada's, her eyebrows like moth antennae;
her smile dimples sweetly, her bright eyes are clear in black and white.
The tall beauty is stately; she halts in the farm outskirts.
The four stallions are proud, the red cloth on their bits flutters;
in a carriage screened with pheasant feathers she goes to court; grandees, withdraw early,
so as not to tire our lord.
The Yellow River is wide, flowing north with a rush;
nets are cast with a splash, sturgeon and pike leap and flash;
reeds and rushes stand tall, the Jiang ladies are tall and fine,
and the officers are strong and stately.

glossary.note: A woman of tall, slender build.
A thin linen coat worn over other clothes.
The tender shoots of thatch grass, describing fine, soft fingers.
The white, long larva of a longhorn beetle, used for a neck.
The white, even seeds of a gourd, used for teeth.

glossary.en: qin shou e mei - cicada brow, moth eyebrows
glossary.note: The qin is a small cicada with a square forehead; e mei are the slender curved antennae of a silkworm moth.

glossary.en: qiao xiao qian xi, mei mu pan xi - smile and eyes
glossary.note: Qian is a pretty dimple; pan is clear black and white in the eye.

glossary.en: shu Jiang - the ladies of the Jiang family
glossary.note: The women of the Jiang surname who came with the bride as attendants.

shuoren.background: The Mao Preface says it grieves for Zhuang Jiang, because Duke Zhuang favoured a concubine and Zhuang Jiang, though virtuous, had no son; the Zuo Commentary records that the people of Wei made the poem for her. Writers and painters later used the many images for each part of a woman's body.

mang.summary: A poem of the Wei Airs in the voice of a woman cast off by her husband. She tells the whole course from courtship to marriage, hard work as a wife, his change of heart and ill-treatment, her brothers not understanding, and her final break. The narrative is complete and the feeling sorrowful; it is one of the earliest long poems about an abandoned wife in China.
mang.translation:
The man came all smiles, carrying cloth to trade for silk.
He did not come to trade for silk; he came to plan with me.
I saw you off across the Qi, as far as Dunqiu.
It was not I who delayed; you had no good go-between.
Please, do not be angry: let us set autumn as the time.
I climbed that broken wall to look towards Fuguan.
When I did not see Fuguan, my tears fell in streams.
When I saw Fuguan, I laughed and I talked.
You consulted tortoise and stalks, and they said nothing unlucky.
Bring your carriage and I will move with my dowry.
Before the mulberry has shed its leaves, they are glossy and lush.
Ah, doves, do not eat the mulberries.
Ah, girls, do not dally with men.
If a man dallies, he can still make excuses;
if a woman dallies, she cannot.
When the mulberry leaves fall, they turn yellow and drop.
Since I went to you, for three years I have eaten poverty.
The Qi flows broad and swift, soaking the carriage curtains.
I did not go wrong; the man was double in his conduct.
The man has no standard; he is inconstant in virtue.
For three years I was a wife; no household task but was toil.
Up early and to bed late, never a morning's rest.
Once he had what he wanted, he turned cruel.
My brothers do not know; they only laugh at me.
Quietly I think it over, and grieve for myself.
To grow old with you - old age only brings me bitterness.
The Qi has its banks, the marsh has its shore.
In the happy days when we wore our hair in tufts, we talked and laughed gently.
Our oaths were sincere and bright; I never thought they would be reversed.
Not thinking of reversal - now it is over.

glossary.note: Originally 'a commoner'; here the man in the poem.

glossary.en: chi chi - simple and honest, or smiling
glossary.note: The look of an honest fellow; one view says smiling.
To exchange.

glossary.en: qian qi - to delay the date
glossary.note: To put off the wedding day.

glossary.en: gui yuan - a broken wall (pronounced gui yuan)
glossary.note: A ruined wall.

glossary.en: Fuguan - the man's home, or the man
glossary.note: The man's dwelling, or the man himself.

glossary.en: er bu er shi - you consulted tortoise and stalks
glossary.note: Divination before the wedding to see whether the match was lucky.

glossary.en: zong jiao zhi yan - the happy days of childhood hair-tufts
glossary.note: Zong jiao is the way children tied their hair in two tufts; the line means happy times in youth.

mang.background: The Mao Preface says it mocks the age: under Duke Xuan of Wei ritual and rightness were gone, licence was rife, and men and women had no proper distinctions, hence this poem of an abandoned wife; Zhu Xi called it the account of a woman who had run off and then been abandoned. Modern readers all see it as a poem of the abandoned wife. The mulberry leaves lush and then fallen stand for a woman's rise and fall. It also criticises the unequal treatment of men and women, and is seen as a leading narrative poem of the Book of Songs.

zhugan.summary: A poem of the Wei Airs of a Wei woman married far away who longs for her home and family. The fishing rod and the River Qi open it. She wants to visit her parents but cannot, and only sails out to ease her sorrow. The tone is tender and restrained.
zhugan.translation:
Long, slim bamboo rod, for fishing in the Qi.
How could I not think of you? It is far and I cannot reach you.
The Spring-source is on the left, the Qi on the right.
A girl who marries goes far from her brothers and parents.
The Qi is on the right, the Spring-source on the left.
A bright smile showing white teeth, jade pendants swaying in step.
The Qi flows on and on; with cypress oars in a pine boat,
I set out to sail and pour away my sorrow.

glossary.en: ti ti - long and slim (pronounced ti)
glossary.note: Slender and upright.

glossary.en: qi bu er si - how could I not think of you?
glossary.note: A rhetorical question: of course I think of you.

glossary.en: yuan mo zhi zhi - too far to reach
glossary.note: The road is long and she cannot get there.

glossary.en: you xing - to go away to marry
glossary.note: To leave home to be married.

glossary.en: cuo - showing white teeth when smiling
glossary.note: The look of bright teeth when one laughs.

glossary.en: nuo - walking in time with grace
glossary.note: A graceful, rhythmic walk.

glossary.en: you you - flowing on without end
glossary.note: The look of water flowing without stopping.

glossary.en: gui ji song zhou - cypress oars, pine boat
glossary.note: Oars of cypress and a boat of pine, meaning a fine vessel.

zhugan.background: The Mao Preface says it is about a woman of Wei who longed to visit her parents but could not, and Zhu Xi's view is close. Modern readers also take it as the homesick song of a woman married far away. The Qi, a mark of Wei, appears also in 'A Man' and 'Qi Ao'.

heguang.summary: A poem of the Wei Airs in which someone in Wei misses Song, saying with exaggeration that the River is not wide and Song is not far, to show how strongly they long to return. Its conception is fresh and clever; each stanza has four lines in crisp language.
heguang.translation:
Who says the River is wide? A single reed will cross it.
Who says Song is far? On tiptoe I can see it.
Who says the River is wide? It will not even hold a little boat.
Who says Song is far? One would not take a morning to get there.

glossary.note: The Yellow River.

glossary.en: yi wei hang zhi - a single reed will cross it
glossary.note: Hang is the same as 'to sail'; a bundle of reeds made into a little raft would carry one over.

glossary.en: qi - to stand on tiptoe (pronounced qi)
glossary.note: To raise oneself on the toes.

glossary.en: zeng bu rong dao - it will not hold a small boat
glossary.note: Dao stands for a small boat; the river is so narrow that no boat would fit.
The time from dawn to the morning meal, a short while.

heguang.background: The Mao Preface says it was written by the mother of Duke Xiang of Song, who had been sent home to Wei and missed her son; Zhu Xi says it was the wife of Duke Huan of Song who returned to Wei and missed her son in Song. Most take this view today, or read the poem as a general song of homesickness.

boxi.summary: A poem of the Wei Airs in which a woman thinks of her husband, away on the eastern campaign. She has no heart to dress, is content to have a headache from longing, and cannot find a herb of forgetfulness. She first praises him as a brave man, then shows herself worn down, using comparison and rhetorical questions with sincere, deep feeling.
boxi.translation:
My lord is tall and mighty, a hero of the state.
My lord carries a lance, leading the king's vanguard.
Since my lord went east, my hair has been like tumbleweed.
Do I lack oil and washwater? For whom would I make myself fair?
Rain, rain, I hope - but the sun comes out bright.
I long and think of my lord, content to have a sore head.
Where can I find the herb of forgetting? I would plant it behind the house.
I long and think of my lord, and it sickens my heart.

glossary.en: bo - 'elder brother', a wife's word for her husband
glossary.note: Bo originally meant the eldest of brothers; wives of old used it for their husbands.
A stately, martial look.

glossary.en: jie - hero (the same as another word for 'hero')
glossary.note: An outstanding man.
A long weapon of bamboo or wood.
Dried fleabane that rolls in the wind, used for tangled hair.

glossary.en: gao mu - hair oil and washwater
glossary.note: The oil for the hair and the water for washing it.
The day-lily, called the herb that makes one forget sorrow.

glossary.en: mei - to sicken with grief (pronounced mei)
glossary.note: To be made ill by worry.

boxi.background: The Mao Preface says it mocks the times: a gentleman is away too long on service and his wife longs for him. Zhu Xi said it was a wife writing because her husband was the king's vanguard. Modern readers all see it as a poem of a wife left behind. 'Hair like tumbleweed' and 'for whom would I make myself fair' became stock phrases for a woman who misses her man.

mugua.summary: A poem of the Wei Airs on gifts exchanged between lovers or friends. A quince is thrown and fine jade given back, yet 'it was not to repay' - the point is lasting friendship, so feeling counts for more than the thing. Three stanzas repeat.
mugua.translation:
You threw me a quince, and I returned a fine jade pendant.
It was not to repay you, but so we may be friends for ever.
You threw me a peach-like quince, and I returned a fine jade ring.
It was not to repay you, but so we may be friends for ever.
You threw me a plum-like quince, and I returned fine jade beads.
It was not to repay you, but so we may be friends for ever.

glossary.note: A sour fruit of the rose family, not the papaya of today.
Beautiful jade; ju is a pendant jade.
Both are names of beautiful jade.

glossary.en: mu tao, mu li - peach-like and plum-like quince
glossary.note: Fruits of the same family as the quince, also sour.
It was not done as repayment.

glossary.en: yong yi wei hao - to be friends for ever
glossary.note: To make lasting friendship.

mugua.background: The Mao Preface thinks it praises Duke Huan of Qi for helping Wei, which the people of Wei wanted to repay; Zhu Xi called it a poem of gifts between a man and a woman. Modern readers mostly take it as a poem of showing feeling by gifts between lovers or friends. The later saying 'throw a quince, get back jade' means to exchange a little for a lot, a little different from the original.

shuli.summary: A poem of the Royal Airs: a traveller passes the old capital and finds the former palaces now fields of millet; in grief he cries out to Heaven. Three stanzas move from sprouts to ears to grain, hinting at passing time, while his heart goes from unsteady to drunken to choked. Later this was called the 'sorrow of the millet'.
shuli.translation:
There the broomcorn millet hangs in rows, there the foxtail millet is in shoots.
I walk on slowly, my heart unsteady.
Those who know me say my heart is troubled;
those who do not ask what I am seeking.
O far blue Heaven, who has done this?
There the broomcorn millet hangs in rows, there the foxtail millet is in ear.
I walk on slowly, my heart as if drunk.
Those who know me say my heart is troubled;
those who do not ask what I am seeking.
O far blue Heaven, who has done this?
There the broomcorn millet hangs in rows, there the foxtail millet is in grain.
I walk on slowly, my heart as if choked.
Those who know me say my heart is troubled;
those who do not ask what I am seeking.
O far blue Heaven, who has done this?

glossary.en: shu, ji - two kinds of millet
glossary.note: Shu is sticky broomcorn millet; ji is generally foxtail millet (some say sorghum).
Thick, with heads drooping.
To go on a journey.
Dragging.
Within the heart.
Uneasy in spirit.
Food stuck in the throat; so grief that one cannot speak.
Distant and vast.

shuli.background: The Mao Preface says a grandee of Zhou came to the old capital Haojing and saw the ancestral temples and palaces all turned to millet fields, so he grieved for the fall of the Zhou house and wrote this poem. This is the account most widely known, and 'the millet' became a symbol of grief for a fallen state. Some modern readers think it is simply the ordinary sadness of a traveller and not necessarily about a fallen state.

junziyuyi.summary: A poem of the Royal Airs: at dusk a wife sees the hens go to roost and the sheep and cattle come home, and thinks of her husband far away on service. The homely evening scene sets off his not being able to return. Plain in language, it is a well-known mix of evocation and statement.
junziyuyi.translation:
My lord is away on service; I do not know when it will end.
When will he come?
The hens roost in their holes in the wall;
the day is drawing to its close,
and the sheep and cattle come down.
My lord is away on service - how could I not think of him?
My lord is away on service, beyond counting days and months.
When shall we meet?
The hens roost on their perches;
the day is drawing to its close,
and the sheep and cattle are gathered in.
My lord is away on service - may he suffer neither hunger nor thirst.

glossary.note: Gone out for military or labour service.
At what time.

glossary.en: shi - a hole in a wall for hens (pronounced shi)
glossary.note: A chicken roost dug into a wall.
To come down from the slope.

glossary.en: bu ri bu yue - beyond days and months
glossary.note: Time that can no longer be counted, meaning a very long while.
To come together.
A wooden frame on which hens roost.
Sheep and cattle collected in their pens at night; kuo means to gather.

junziyuyi.background: The Mao Preface says it mocks King Ping: a gentleman was on service for no set time and the grandees worried about his danger; Zhu Xi said a wife was thinking of her husband away on service. Today it is read as a poem of a woman missing her man, and its dusk scene became a model for later poems of longing.

yangzhishui.summary: A poem of the Royal Airs, a song of garrison soldiers who long for home and resent the unfairness of the postings. The slow water that cannot move even a bundle of firewood sets the scene: people are kept apart and duties are uneven. In three stanzas the soldier sighs again and again, 'in which month shall I go home?'
yangzhishui.translation:
The water, so slow, will not carry even a bundle of firewood.
That man does not come with me to guard Shen.
I long for home, I long for home!
In which month shall I go back?
The water, so slow, will not carry even a bundle of thorn-wood.
That man does not come with me to guard Fu.
I long for home, I long for home!
In which month shall I go back?
The water, so slow, will not carry even a bundle of rushes.
That man does not come with me to guard Xu.
I long for home, I long for home!
In which month shall I go back?

glossary.en: yang zhi shui - slow, weak water
glossary.note: Water flowing gently and feebly.

glossary.en: shu xin - a bundle of firewood
glossary.note: A bundle of brushwood.

glossary.en: bi qi zhi zi - that man
glossary.note: That person: someone who stays home and is not made to garrison, or someone back at home.
To guard a frontier post.

glossary.en: Shen, Fu, Xu - three states of the Jiang clan
glossary.note: Shen lay near present-day Nanyang in Henan, Fu is the same as Lu, and Xu lay near present-day Xuchang in Henan.
To think of with yearning.
When.

yangzhishui.background: The Mao Preface says it criticises King Ping of Zhou for not caring for his people and sending men to guard his mother's home state, Shen, far away, which the Zhou people resented; Zhu Xi agreed. Most readers today take it as a song of a conscript who wants to go home. King Ping's mother came from Shen, which gives the line about guarding Shen.

caige.summary: A poem of the Royal Airs about lovers longing for each other. In three stanzas only the plant picked and the length of time change, from three months to three autumns to three years, so that one day apart feels very long; it is both moving and exaggerated, and the sayings 'a day is like three autumns' come from it.
caige.translation:
He is out picking kudzu; a day without seeing him is like three months.
He is out picking wormwood; a day without seeing him is like three autumns.
He is out picking mugwort; a day without seeing him is like three years.

glossary.note: A climbing vine whose fibre is woven into cloth.
A sweet-smelling artemisia used in ancient sacrifices.
Used for medicine and for making moxa.

glossary.en: san yue, san qiu, san sui - three months, three autumns, three years
glossary.note: Three months; three autumns (which means three years); three years. They show how deep the longing is and how hard the time is to bear.
He, the one thought of.

caige.background: The Mao Preface says it was made out of fear when slanders were in power; Zhu Xi called it a poem of licentious elopement. Modern readers all agree it is a love poem about missing the beloved. 'A day without seeing you is like three autumns apart' has become a common phrase in Chinese.

jiangzhongzi.summary: A poem of the Zheng Airs in which a girl, in love but afraid of her parents, brothers and the neighbours' gossip, begs her lover not to climb the wall or break the trees. Each stanza adds weight, drawing the conflict between love and fear with fine, true detail.
jiangzhongzi.translation:
I beg you, Zhongzi, do not climb into my village lane,
do not break my willow trees.
Do I begrudge them? I fear my father and mother.
Zhong, I do long for you,
but my parents' words are also to be feared.
I beg you, Zhongzi, do not climb over my wall,
do not break my mulberry trees.
Do I begrudge them? I fear my brothers.
Zhong, I do long for you,
but my brothers' words are also to be feared.
I beg you, Zhongzi, do not climb into my garden,
do not break my sandalwood trees.
Do I begrudge them? I fear people's many words.
Zhong, I do long for you,
but people's many words are also to be feared.

glossary.note: A word of request: 'please, Zhongzi'.
A man of second birth order; here the girl's name for her lover.
A cluster of homes in old times; here the gate of the lane.
A kind of willow.

glossary.en: huai - to think of with longing
glossary.note: To miss and long for.
To dread, to take care about.

glossary.en: ren zhi duo yan - what people say
glossary.note: The talk and gossip of others.

jiangzhongzi.background: The Mao Preface says it mocks Duke Zhuang of Zheng for giving way to his younger brother Shu Duan of Gong; Zhu Xi took it as the work of someone 'running off'. Modern readers all see it as a girl turning away her lover's rash courtship, showing how she is torn between love and propriety and public opinion.

nvyuejiming.summary: A poem of the Zheng Airs, entirely a dialogue between husband and wife: at dawn she urges him up to go hunting, and the poem pictures their life afterwards of food, wine and music, with a gift of jade as a sign of affection. It is warm and harmonious, one of the loveliest descriptions of married life in the Book of Songs.
nvyuejiming.translation:
The woman says, "The cock has crowed"; the man says, "It is barely dawn."
"Get up and look at the night: the morning star is blazing.
You will roam and range, and shoot wild duck and geese.
When you have shot them, I will cook them for you.
Cooked, we will drink wine, and grow old together.
With zither and lute at hand, all is peaceful and good."
"If I know you are coming to me, I will give you my mixed jade pendants.
If I know you are gentle with me, I will present you with my mixed jade pendants.
If I know you love me, I will repay you with my mixed jade pendants."

glossary.en: zi xing shi ye - you, get up and look at the night
glossary.note: Zi is 'you', the husband.

glossary.en: ming xing you lan - the bright star is blazing
glossary.note: The morning star shines; lan is bright.

glossary.en: yi - to shoot with a corded arrow (pronounced yi)
glossary.note: To hunt with an arrow tied to a cord.
A wild duck.
To prepare as food; another view takes it to mean 'be in harmony'.
To play or have at hand.
A pendant made of several pieces of jade.

glossary.en: wen - to present as a gift
glossary.note: To give.

nvyuejiming.background: The Mao Preface says it criticises a ruler who does not love virtue but loves beauty; Zhu Xi says it is the words of a worthy couple warning each other. Today it is read as a love poem between husband and wife, rare in the Book of Songs for telling family life through dialogue. The words 「琴瑟在御，莫不靜好」 ("with zither and lute at hand, all is peaceful and good") became a famous blessing for a harmonious couple.

younvtongche.summary: A poem of the Zheng Airs: a man rides in the same carriage with a girl of the Jiang clan and praises her face like hibiscus, her graceful movement, her chiming jade and her good character. It is a song for a wedding or the groom's fetching the bride. Two stanzas repeat.

glossary.en: tong che - to share a carriage
glossary.note: To ride in one carriage, which at a wedding means the groom and bride.
The rose of Sharon, which opens in the morning and fades by evening.

glossary.en: jiang ao jiang xiang - as if soaring and gliding
glossary.note: A light, bird-like way of walking.
Beautiful jade; ju is a pendant jade.

glossary.en: Meng Jiang - the eldest Jiang daughter
glossary.note: Meng means eldest and Jiang is the family name; here it means a beautiful woman in general.
Refined and lovely.

glossary.en: qiang qiang - the sound of pendants (pronounced qiang qiang)
glossary.note: The ring of jade pendants striking together.

glossary.en: de yin - good name, fair words
glossary.note: A good reputation or good speech.

younvtongche.background: The Mao Preface says it mocks Hu of Zheng for not marrying a daughter of Qi and so losing the help of a great state; Zhu Xi called it a poem of licentious elopement. Today most read it as a song for fetching the bride, praising her. 'Meng Jiang' later became a stock name for a beauty.

chuqidongmen.summary: A poem of the Zheng Airs: a man goes out by the east gate and sees girls like clouds, but loves only his wife in plain white clothes and an old kerchief. It praises faithfulness and a poor couple's love. Two stanzas repeat.
chuqidongmen.translation:
I go out by the east gate; the girls are many as clouds.
Many as clouds, but none is the one I think of.
In white silk and a grey-green kerchief - she alone delights me.
I go out by the curving gate; the girls are like white reed blossoms.
Many as reed blossoms, but none is the one I long for.
In white silk and a madder-red kerchief - she is the one I can be happy with.

glossary.note: Very many.

glossary.en: fei wo si cun - not the one my thoughts dwell on
glossary.note: Not where my mind is, not the one I long for.

glossary.en: gao yi - plain white silk dress
glossary.note: An undyed white silk dress, worn by girls from poor homes.
A grey-green cloth worn at a woman's belt, also plain dress.
A helping word; one view says it is 'say'.

glossary.en: yin du - a curved gate tower
glossary.note: The crescent-shaped outer wall of a city gate.
The white flower of the thatch reed, used for a great crowd of girls.
A dye plant that gives a deep red.

chuqidongmen.background: The Mao Preface says it grieves at disorder, when princes fought for the throne, arms never rested, and husbands and wives deserted one another; Zhu Xi said that people saw how many women there were but a husband and wife could not keep each other safe. Most today read it as a love poem praising faithfulness in marriage. The line 「出其東門，有女如雲」 ("I go out by the east gate; the girls are many as clouds") is often quoted.

yeyoumancao.summary: A poem of the Zheng Airs: in a field of dew-wet grass a man meets by chance a girl with clear eyes and lovely brows, is struck at once and feels it is just as he wished. The theme of meeting by chance is common in the Songs. Two stanzas repeat in fresh language.
yeyoumancao.translation:
In the fields grows creeping grass, heavy with falling dew.
There is one lovely person, with clear eyes and fine brows.
We meet by chance, just as I wished.
In the fields grows creeping grass, with dew thick on it.
There is one lovely person, graceful with clear eyes and fine brows.
We meet by chance, and are happy together.

glossary.note: Dew that has settled.
The look of much dew.

glossary.en: qing yang - clear eyes and fine brows
glossary.note: Qing is clear of eye; yang is lifted brows.
Fair and soft.

glossary.en: xie hou - to meet by chance
glossary.note: An unplanned meeting.

glossary.en: shi wo yuan - just as I wished
glossary.note: It fits what I hoped for.

glossary.en: rang rang - thick with dew (pronounced rang rang)
glossary.note: The look of abundant dew.
Good and fine.

yeyoumancao.background: The Mao Preface says it longs for a time of meeting: the ruler's kindness did not reach down, the people were worn out by war, and men and women missed their season, so they longed for chance meetings. Modern readers mostly take it as a love song about a chance meeting. 'Xie hou' later became a common word for a casual encounter.

qinwei.summary: A poem of the Zheng Airs about young men and women playing together by the Zhen and Wei rivers in spring, joking and giving each other peonies. Told as a conversation between a girl and a boy, it has the feel of a folk festival with song and dance.
qinwei.translation:
The Zhen and the Wei are in full spring flow.
Young men and women hold orchids.
The girl says, "Shall we look?" The man says, "I have already been."
"Go and look again, beyond the Wei;
it is truly wide, and pleasant."
So the men and women tease each other,
and give each other peonies.
The Zhen and the Wei run deep and clear.
Young men and women fill the banks.
The girl says, "Shall we look?" The man says, "I have already been."
"Go and look again, beyond the Wei;
it is truly wide, and pleasant."
So the men and women joke together,
and give each other peonies.

glossary.en: Zhen, Wei - the Zhen and Wei rivers
glossary.note: Two rivers in the Xinzheng area of present-day Henan.
The look of a great spring flood.
A kind of orchid; people carried it at the Shangsi festival to ward off evil.
Ju is the same as 'to go'; they have already gone.
Truly broad; xu means large.

glossary.en: xiang xue - to tease each other
glossary.note: To joke with one another.
Peonies; giving a peony was a sign of friendship or a promise.
The look of deep, clear water.

qinwei.background: The Mao Preface says it mocks disorder; Zhu Xi took it as the words of lovers eloping. Modern readers say it describes the Shangsi spring outing, with purification and courtship, and keeps a folk custom of Zheng in Zhou times.

fengyu.summary: A poem of the Zheng Airs: amid wind and rain and crowing cocks, the speaker at last meets the one longed for, and the joy is beyond words. The storm and the cocks set the mood, and three stanzas build from peace of mind, to cure, to gladness.
fengyu.translation:
Wind and rain are cold and chill; the cocks crow clear.
Now that I have seen my lord, how could my heart not be at peace?
Wind and rain beat down; the cocks crow loud.
Now that I have seen my lord, how could I not be cured?
Wind and rain are dark as night; the cocks crow without ceasing.
Now that I have seen my lord, how could I not be glad?

glossary.note: Cool, bitter.

glossary.en: jie jie - the crowing of a cock
glossary.note: The sound of a cock crowing.

glossary.en: jun zi - my lord, the gentleman
glossary.note: The one the speaker longs for; it can be a husband or a lover.
'How could it be that'.
Level, calm in mind.

glossary.en: xiao xiao - beating down (of wind and rain)
glossary.note: The look of fast wind and rain.
To recover from illness.
As dim as night.

fengyu.background: The Mao Preface says it longs for a gentleman who in a chaotic age does not change his principles; Zhu Xi called it an elopement poem. Today many read it as a song of husband and wife or lovers meeting after a long parting. 'Wind and rain dark as night, the cocks crow without ceasing' was later often used of a person of principle in dark times.

zijin.summary: A poem of the Zheng Airs: a girl waits on the city tower for her lover, anxious and resentful that he neither comes nor sends word. The last lines, 「一日不見，如三月兮」 ("a day without seeing you feels like three months"), are famous; Cao Cao quotes the first two lines in his Short Song.
zijin.translation:
Your collar is blue-green, and my heart is long with longing.
Even if I do not go to you, could you not send word?
Your pendant ribbon is blue-green, and my thoughts go on and on.
Even if I do not go to you, could you not come?
Pacing to and fro on the city tower,
a day without seeing you feels like three months.

glossary.note: Zi is 'you'; jin is the same as the word for collar.
The colour of green-blue.
Longing that goes on and on.
Si means to carry on, to send.
The belt-cord for jade pendants.

glossary.en: tao xi ta xi - pacing to and fro
glossary.note: Walking back and forth, hesitating.

glossary.en: cheng que - the towers at the city gate
glossary.note: The watch-towers beside a gate, from which one can see far.

zijin.background: The Mao Preface says it mocks the decay of schools, with students scattering; Zhu Xi called it an elopement poem. Most today see it as a love poem. 'Qing qing zi jin' later came to mean a scholar, because the blue-green collar was a student's dress in old times.

jiming.summary: A poem of the Qi Airs: a morning dialogue by the bed, where the wife says the cock has crowed and the court is full while the husband lingers, taking the cock's crow for flies and the dawn for moonlight. It is lively and funny, mixing scolding with care.
jiming.translation:
"The cock has crowed; the court is already full."
"That is not the cock crowing; it is the buzzing of flies."
"The east is bright; the court is in full swing."
"That is not the east brightening; it is the light of the moon."
"Insects fly humming; I would gladly dream on with you."
"The court is about to break up and go home - do not let them hate me because of you!"

glossary.en: chao ji ying yi - the court is full already
glossary.note: Chao is the court; ying is full, meaning the officials have all arrived.
Not.
Full of life, meaning the court is busy.

glossary.en: hong hong - the hum of insects (pronounced hong)
glossary.note: The sound of a swarm of insects flying.

glossary.en: gan yu zi tong meng - gladly dream with you
glossary.note: Glad to sleep and dream on beside you.

glossary.en: hui qie gui yi - the court is about to break up
glossary.note: The meeting will end soon and people go home.
A word meaning 'hope', 'cause'; the line means do not make people hate you and me.

jiming.background: The Mao Preface says it longs for a worthy queen: the king was lazy in governing and the queen warned him to rise early for court; Zhu Xi agreed. Some modern readers instead take it as a dialogue between a common couple getting up. Because the tone of the speakers is hard to assign, scholars differ a little on who says which lines.

dongfangzhiri.summary: A poem of the Qi Airs in which a man sees his lover as bright as sun and moon lighting his room, following him into his house. The sun and moon as comparisons carry the joy of passionate love. Two short stanzas repeat.
dongfangzhiri.translation:
The sun in the east -
that lovely one
is in my room, is in my room;
she treads in my steps, close to me.
The moon in the east -
that lovely one
is at my door, is at my door;
she treads in my steps as I go.

glossary.note: A fair woman.

glossary.en: bi shu zhe zi - that lovely one
glossary.note: That beautiful person.

glossary.en: zai wo shi xi - in my room
glossary.note: Inside my house.

glossary.en: lu wo ji - treading in my steps, coming close
glossary.note: Lu is to tread; ji is to come near.
The space within a door.

glossary.en: lu wo fa - following me as I leave
glossary.note: Fa means to go, to set out.

dongfangzhiri.background: The Mao Preface says it mocks a decline: ruler and ministers had lost the Way, men and women eloped, and ritual could not reform them; Zhu Xi called it an elopement poem. Today it is read as a love poem, either the man praising his lover or a bride's entry into her husband's home.

fatan.summary: A poem of the Wei Airs in which working people question the nobles who live without working. The toil of cutting sandalwood is set against the nobles' wealth in a string of rhetorical questions with a ringing rhythm. A leading satire in the Book of Songs, in plain statement with a strong edge.
fatan.translation:
Kan-kan we fell the sandalwood,
and set it on the river bank;
the river water is clear and rippling.
You neither sow nor reap,
so why take the grain of three hundred households?
You neither hunt nor trap,
so why do I see badgers hanging in your yard?
Those gentlemen
do not eat for nothing!
Kan-kan we fell wood for wheel spokes,
and set it by the river side;
the river water is clear and straight.
You neither sow nor reap,
so why take three hundred bundles of grain?
You neither hunt nor trap,
so why do I see three-year-old beasts hanging in your yard?
Those gentlemen
do not eat for nothing!
Kan-kan we fell wood for wheels,
and set it at the river brink;
the river water is clear with rolling ripples.
You neither sow nor reap,
so why take the grain of three hundred granaries?
You neither hunt nor trap,
so why do I see quail hanging in your yard?
Those gentlemen
do not eat a free meal!

glossary.en: kan kan - the sound of chopping
glossary.note: The noise of an axe on wood.

glossary.en: zhi - to put, to set down
glossary.note: To place.
The river bank.

glossary.en: jia se - to sow and to reap
glossary.note: Jia is planting crops; se is harvesting.
The fields and house of one family; three hundred chan means the harvest of three hundred households.
A badger; another view says a young raccoon dog.

glossary.en: su can - to eat for nothing
glossary.note: To live on food one has not earned.
A round grain store.

fatan.background: The Mao Preface says it mocks greed: those in office were greedy and base and took without working, so gentlemen could not rise; Zhu Xi said the woodcutters were stating their own aims, not envying the rich. Today it is usually read as the people's satire on exploiters, though some think the closing line 「彼君子兮，不素餐兮」 ("those gentlemen do not eat for nothing") is meant ironically.

shuoshu.summary: A poem of the Wei Airs in which the people compare their heavy-taxing rulers to a greedy rat and say they will leave to look for a happy land. Three stanzas, from 'happy land' to 'happy state' to 'happy outskirts', express their longing for a life of peace and work; it works by comparison.
