shuoshu.translation:
Big rat, big rat, do not eat my millet!
Three years I have served you, and you would not look after me.
I swear I will leave you and go to that happy land.
Happy land, happy land, there I shall find my place.
Big rat, big rat, do not eat my wheat!
Three years I have served you, and you would not be kind to me.
I swear I will leave you and go to that happy state.
Happy state, happy state, there I shall find what is right.
Big rat, big rat, do not eat my sprouts!
Three years I have served you, and you would not comfort me.
I swear I will leave you and go to those happy outskirts.
Happy outskirts, happy outskirts, who would wail there for ever?

glossary.note: A large rat.
To wait on, to provide for.
The same as 'you'.

glossary.en: mo wo ken gu - you would not look after me
glossary.note: You would not care for me.
A borrowed form of 'to swear'; another view takes it as 'go'.
To go, to head for.

glossary.en: yuan de wo suo - there I find my place
glossary.note: I get a place to settle.

glossary.en: yong hao - to wail for long
glossary.note: To cry out and sigh over a long time.

shuoshu.background: The Mao Preface says it mocks heavy taxes: the people criticised their ruler for gnawing at them like silkworms and not governing well; Zhu Xi was similar. Modern readers see it as the work of peasants resisting exploitation and longing for an ideal society. 'Big rat' later became a common way to describe corrupt officials.

xishuai.summary: A poem of the Tang Airs: at year's end, when crickets come indoors, it urges people to prize their time and enjoy themselves, but without neglecting their duties or sinking into pleasure. Three stanzas, from the year's close to its going, show the careful, thrifty habits of the people of Jin.
xishuai.translation:
The cricket is in the hall; the year is drawing to its close.
If I do not enjoy myself now, the days and months will pass away.
But let ease not go too far; always think of your duty.
Love pleasure but do not go wild; a good man is watchful.
The cricket is in the hall; the year is going.
If I do not enjoy myself now, the days and months will go by.
But let ease not go too far; always think of what lies beyond.
Love pleasure but do not go wild; a good man is brisk and diligent.
The cricket is in the hall; the work carts are at rest.
If I do not enjoy myself now, the days and months will slip away.
But let ease not go too far; always think of the troubles.
Love pleasure but do not go wild; a good man is calm and at ease.

glossary.note: A helping word.
Late, meaning the end of the year.
To pass by and be gone.

glossary.en: wu yi da kang - do not take too much ease
glossary.note: Yi means 'too'; da kang means excessive comfort.

glossary.en: zhi si qi ju - always think of your place
glossary.note: Ju is one's position and duty.
Looking about alertly.
Hard-working and nimble.
A cart for service or hauling, which rests only in the slack season.

xishuai.background: The Mao Preface says it mocks Duke Xi of Jin for being thrifty beyond the rites; Zhu Xi said it was a folk song of enjoying oneself at year's end without forgetting ritual. Modern readers also call it a year-end song urging people to enjoy life with moderation. 'The cricket is in the hall' often stands for the end of the year.

shanyoushu.summary: A poem of the Tang Airs, opening with the thorn elm on the hill and the elm in the marsh, urging people to use their goods while they live or after death others will have them. The tone is blunt, a satire on misers that also sighs at the shortness of life.
shanyoushu.translation:
On the hill is the thorn elm, in the marsh the elm.
You have robes, but do not trail them or wear them.
You have carriages and horses, but do not drive or ride them.
Once you are dead, someone else will enjoy them.
On the hill is the kao tree, in the marsh the niu.
You have courtyard and halls, but do not sprinkle or sweep them.
You have bells and drums, but do not sound or strike them.
Once you are dead, someone else will keep them.
On the hill is the lacquer tree, in the marsh the chestnut.
You have wine and food - why not play the zither every day?
Take your pleasure, and make the day long.
Once you are dead, someone else will enter your house.

glossary.note: A prickly kind of elm.
Low and wet land.

glossary.en: ye, lu - to trail, to wear
glossary.note: Ye is to drag one's robe along; lou is to pull on, in general to wear.
The look of death; another view reads it as 'if'.
Delight, here other people's enjoying of it.

glossary.en: kao, niu - two kinds of tree
glossary.note: Kao is a mountain ailanthus; niu is a kind of tree.
To beat.
To keep.

shanyoushu.background: The Mao Preface says it mocks Duke Zhao of Jin, who could not order his state and could not use his wealth; Zhu Xi says someone else wrote it on seeing that the man could not enjoy himself. Today it is read as a poem of advice, or mockery of the hoarder, and some see in it anxiety about death.

chelin.summary: A poem of the Qin Airs describing the grandeur of the ruler's carriages and music at the Qin court, and the joy of sitting beside the lord playing the zither and the reed organ. Starting with chariots and eunuchs, it turns to the sigh 「今者不樂，逝者其耋」 ("if we do not enjoy ourselves now, in time we will be old"), which has both court splendour and a feeling for life's brevity.
chelin.translation:
Chariots rumble, and horses with white foreheads.
Before we see the lord, the eunuch gives the order.
On the slope is lacquer, in the marsh chestnut.
Having seen the lord, we sit side by side and play the zither.
If we do not enjoy ourselves now, in time we will be old.
On the slope are mulberries, in the marsh poplars.
Having seen the lord, we sit side by side and play the reed organ.
If we do not enjoy ourselves now, in time we will be dead.

glossary.en: lin lin - rumbling (the same as lin lin)
glossary.note: The sound of chariots running.
A horse with white hair on its forehead.
An inner attendant at court who passes on the ruler's orders.
A hillside.

glossary.en: gu se - to play the zither
glossary.note: To play the se.

glossary.en: shi zhe qi die - in time, old age (pronounced die)
glossary.note: Shi is 'going', here meaning in future; die is an old person of eighty, so old age in general.
The reed of a mouth organ; here to play such an instrument.
Death.

chelin.background: The Mao Preface says it praises Qin Zhong, who was beginning to grow strong and had the good things of carriages, horses, rites and music; Zhu Xi was similar. It is one of the earliest poems to show the Qin court. Tradition says Qin began as a western border state under Zhou and only later grew strong.

huangniao.summary: A poem of the Qin Airs, a lament for three worthy men buried alive with Duke Mu of Qin. The yellow bird settling opens it, and it shows the three men trembling at the grave pit, and a cry to Heaven offering a hundred lives for one. It is an early Chinese protest against human sacrifice.
huangniao.translation:
Jiao-jiao the yellow bird settles on the jujube.
Who follows Duke Mu? Ziju Yanxi.
This Yanxi was the peer of a hundred men.
Facing the grave pit, he trembles in dread.
O blue Heaven, you destroy our good man!
If he could be ransomed, a hundred of us would give our bodies.
Jiao-jiao the yellow bird settles on the mulberry.
Who follows Duke Mu? Ziju Zhonghang.
This Zhonghang was a match for a hundred men.
Facing the grave pit, he trembles in dread.
O blue Heaven, you destroy our good man!
If he could be ransomed, a hundred of us would give our bodies.
Jiao-jiao the yellow bird settles on the thorn.
Who follows Duke Mu? Ziju Qianhu.
This Qianhu was a defence against a hundred men.
Facing the grave pit, he trembles in dread.
O blue Heaven, you destroy our good man!
If he could be ransomed, a hundred of us would give our bodies.

glossary.en: jiao jiao - the call of a bird
glossary.note: The sound of a bird; one view takes it as the look of flying back and forth.
The thorny wild date tree.
Ziju is the family name and Yanxi the personal name; with Zhonghang and Qianhu they are called the 'Three Good Men'.
To match; to stand out.
To hold off, to be equal to.

glossary.en: zhui zhui qi li - trembling with fear
glossary.note: Shaking in terror.
To kill off.
To buy back by giving something; here to give one's own life for the Three Good Men.

huangniao.background: The Mao Preface says this mourns the Three Good Men. According to the Zuo Commentary, after Duke Mu of Qin died the three sons of the Ziju clan were buried with him, and the people grieved and composed 'Yellow Bird'. It is an important record of the custom of human burial, showing people's grief at the loss of good men and their dislike of the practice.

jianjia.summary: A poem of the Qin Airs: on the water's edge in late autumn the poet seeks 'that one', who is across the water, seemingly near but never reached. Three stanzas, with a vast landscape and a faint feeling, the airy mood is one of the most symbolic in the Book of Songs.
jianjia.translation:
The reeds are grey-green, white dew has turned to frost.
The one I speak of is on the other side of the water.
I go upstream after her; the road is blocked and long.
I go downstream after her; she seems to be in the middle of the water.
The reeds are lush and thick, the white dew is not yet dry.
The one I speak of is at the water's edge.
I go upstream after her; the road is blocked and steep.
I go downstream after her; she seems to be on a shoal in the water.
The reeds are bright and many, the white dew has not yet gone.
The one I speak of is on the water's bank.
I go upstream after her; the road is blocked and twists to the right.
I go downstream after her; she seems to be on a small islet in the water.

glossary.en: jian jia - reed grass and reeds
glossary.note: Jian is a kind of unheaded reed, jia is the common reed; both are waterside plants.

glossary.en: cang cang, qi qi, cai cai - thick, lush, bright
glossary.note: Words for how thickly the reeds grow.
The person the poem searches for.
To go against the current.
To go with the current.
It seems that.
Dried.

glossary.en: mei, si, chi, zhi - edge, bank, shoal, islet
glossary.note: Mei is where water meets plants; si is the water's edge; chi is a raised shoal in the water; zhi is a small islet.

jianjia.background: The Mao Preface says it mocks Duke Xiang for not following the rites of Zhou; Zhu Xi said he did not know whom it meant. Today most read it as a love poem of seeking a beloved, or the search for a worthy person or an ideal that cannot be reached, with a general symbolic force. 'On the other side of the water' and 'the one I speak of' are often quoted in later love poetry.

wuyi.summary: A battle song of the Qin Airs, sung by soldiers before marching out. Beginning with 「豈曰無衣，與子同袍」 ("who says you have no clothes? I'll share my robe with you"), it shows comrades facing a strong enemy together; the three stanzas build from sharing clothing to shared enmity, shared action and shared march, in a bold spirit.
wuyi.translation:
Who says you have no clothes? I will share my robe with you.
The king is raising troops; I mend my dagger-axe and spear,
and share your enemy.
Who says you have no clothes? I will share my undergarment with you.
The king is raising troops; I mend my spear and halberd,
and rise with you.
Who says you have no clothes? I will share my skirt with you.
The king is raising troops; I mend my armour and weapons,
and march with you.

glossary.en: qi yue wu yi - who says you have no clothes?
glossary.note: A rhetorical question.
The long coat soldiers wore, which also served as a bedcover.

glossary.en: wang yu xing shi - the king is raising troops
glossary.note: Yu is a particle; the king is calling out the army.
To repair and put in order.

glossary.en: tong chou - to share an enemy
glossary.note: To face the same enemy together.
A garment worn next to the skin.
To rise and do things as one.
Helmets, armour and arms.

wuyi.background: The Mao Preface says it mocks the use of troops: the people of Qin criticised their ruler for loving war and not sharing the people's wishes; Zhu Xi said the people of Qin were fierce, glad to fight, and urged each other on. Modern readers mostly take it as a stirring army song. The sayings 'share a hatred of the enemy' and 'comrades' come from this poem.

wanqiu.summary: A poem of the Chen Airs: a man loves a woman dancing on Wanqiu and has no hope of her, yet follows her all year. The first stanza is about her dancing and his hopeless feeling; the other two, with drum, pottery drum and egret feathers, show the dance that goes on in every season.

glossary.note: The person he loves.
The swaying of dance steps.
A low-centred hill in Chen; tradition says a place for rites with song and dance.
Really full of feeling.
No hope of her.
A clay percussion vessel.
Egret plumes, used as dance props.
A dance fan or parasol made of feathers.

wanqiu.background: The Mao Preface says it mocks Duke You for his dissolute wandering; Zhu Xi said it was about roaming and not coming back. Today it is mostly read as a man's love for a dancing priestess. Chen was a state of strong shamanic custom; the History of the Han says Lady Taiji loved sacrifices and the people loved song and dance.

hengmen.summary: A poem of the Chen Airs in which a recluse is content in poverty. With his crossbar gate and a spring to ease his hunger, he says he need not eat Yellow River fish or marry a Jiang of Qi or a Zi of Song; plain food is enough. The language is plain and the thought close to Daoism.
hengmen.translation:
Beneath a crossbar gate, one can rest at ease.
The Bi spring flows wide; it can ease hunger.
When one eats fish, must it be the bream of the Yellow River?
When one takes a wife, must she be a Jiang of Qi?
When one eats fish, must it be the carp of the Yellow River?
When one takes a wife, must she be a Zi of Song?

glossary.en: heng men - a gate of crossbars
glossary.note: A gate of a single crossbar; it describes a humble house.

glossary.en: qi chi - to rest and wander
glossary.note: To loiter, to take ease.
The name of a stream; one view takes it as the look of a flowing spring.
Le is used for 'to cure'; so to cure hunger.
A tasty bream from the Yellow River.

glossary.en: Qi zhi Jiang - a Jiang woman of Qi
glossary.note: A woman of the Jiang clan of Qi, a great noble house.

glossary.en: Song zhi Zi - a Zi woman of Song
glossary.note: A woman of the Zi clan of Song, also noble.

glossary.en: qu - to take a wife (the same as another word)
glossary.note: The same as the word for 'to marry (a wife)'.

hengmen.background: The Mao Preface says it is to lead and help the ruler along; Zhu Xi said it was made by a recluse who was content and wanted nothing. Today it is read as a recluse's poem of contentment in poverty, near Daoist ideas. 'Heng men' and 'qi chi' later often name a hermit's dwelling or a retired life.

yuechu.summary: A poem of the Chen Airs of longing for someone on a moonlit night. Starting with bright moonlight, it uses words such as 'lovely', 'radiant', 'glowing' and 'graceful' for the beauty's looks and walk, and ends in the pain of missing her. The rhythm circles and the scene is misty; it is seen as the start of moon poems in China.
yuechu.translation:
The moon comes out bright; the lovely one is fair,
slow and graceful in her movement; my troubled heart is sore.
The moon comes out white; the lovely one is radiant,
slow and slender in her movement; my troubled heart is restless.
The moon comes out and shines; the lovely one glows,
slow and supple in her movement; my troubled heart is wounded.

glossary.note: Jiao is the same as a word for 'fair'.

glossary.en: liao, liu, liao - fair, radiant, glowing
glossary.note: Three words for beauty, with similar meaning, changed for the rhyme.
Unhurried.

glossary.en: yao jiu, you shou, yao shao - graceful, slender, supple
glossary.note: Three words for a woman's lovely bearing.
A heart weighed with worry and longing.

glossary.en: qiao, sao, can - sore, restless, wounded
glossary.note: All describe sorrow and unrest.

yuechu.background: The Mao Preface says it mocks love of beauty, in that those in office did not love virtue but delighted in beauty; Zhu Xi said it was about a man and woman who delighted in each other and longed for each other. Today it is mostly seen as a love poem written on a moonlit night, with a hazy mood, often called the forerunner of later poems of longing under the moon.

qiyue.summary: The longest poem of the Bin Airs and the longest farming poem in the Book of Songs. Following the seasons it describes a Zhou farmer's year in detail: ploughing, silk, weaving, hunting, wine-making, house-building, storing ice and sacrifice, and also the bitterness of toiling for nobles and still lacking food and clothes. Told in plain statement, it is an important source for Zhou society and the farming calendar.
qiyue.translation:
In the seventh month the Fire star slides west; in the ninth month clothes are handed out.
In the first days the wind howls; in the second days the cold bites.
With no coat and no rough cloth, how can we get through the year?
In the third days we mend the ploughs; in the fourth days we step out to the fields.
With my wife and children I bring food to the southern fields,
and the field overseer comes, pleased.
In the seventh month the Fire star slides west; in the ninth month clothes are handed out.
As the spring days warm, the orioles sing.
The women take their deep baskets and follow the little paths,
to look for tender mulberry leaves.
The spring days are long; many gather the white mugwort.
The women's hearts are sad and sore: they fear being taken away with the lord's son.
In the seventh month the Fire star slides west; in the eighth month the reeds are cut.
In the silkworm month we trim the mulberries; we take axes and hatchets
to chop the far-reaching branches, and strip the young mulberries.
In the seventh month the shrike cries; in the eighth month we spin, dyeing dark and yellow.
My red is very bright - it is made into the lord's son's robe.
In the fourth month the milkwort flowers; in the fifth month the cicada sings;
in the eighth month we harvest; in the tenth month the leaves fall.
In the first days we hunt badger and take fox,
to make furs for the lord's son.
In the second days we gather together, to practise military skills;
the small boars we keep, the big boars we give to the lord.
In the fifth month the grasshopper shakes its legs; in the sixth month the katydid beats its wings;
in the seventh month it is in the fields, in the eighth month under the eaves,
in the ninth month at the door,
in the tenth month the cricket comes under my bed.
We clear the holes and smoke out the rats, stop up the north windows and plaster the doors.
Ah, my wife and children, the year is turning;
come in and live in this house.
In the sixth month we eat plums and wild grapes; in the seventh we boil mallow and beans;
in the eighth month we knock down the dates; in the tenth month we harvest the rice.
We make this spring wine, to wish for long life.
In the seventh month we eat melons; in the eighth month we cut the gourds;
in the ninth month we gather hemp seed,
pick bitter herbs and cut ailanthus for fuel, to feed us farmers.
In the ninth month we make the threshing floor; in the tenth month we bring in the harvest.
Millet, early and late grains, rice, hemp, beans and wheat.
Ah, we farmers - the harvest is all in,
and now we go up to work on the lord's house.
By day you cut thatch, by night you twist rope;
hurry up and roof the house, for soon we sow the hundred grains.
In the second days we chop the ice, chong-chong;
in the third days we store it in the ice-house;
in the fourth days, early in the morning, we offer a lamb and leeks.
In the ninth month the frost is keen; in the tenth month we clear the threshing floor.
We share a feast with two jars of wine, and say: kill the lambs and sheep!
We climb up to the lord's hall and raise the rhino-horn cups:
may you live ten thousand years without end.

glossary.en: liu huo - the Fire star slides west
glossary.note: The star Antares sinks westward at dusk in the seventh month, a sign that the heat is ending.

glossary.en: yi zhi ri, er zhi ri - the first days, the second days
glossary.note: The first and second months of the Zhou calendar, which are the eleventh and twelfth months of the Xia calendar; the third and fourth days are the first and second months of the Xia calendar.

glossary.en: bi fa, li lie - howling, biting cold
glossary.note: Bi fa is the howl of cold wind; li lie is bitter cold.
Coarse garments worn by the poor.
To prune the branches of the mulberry trees.
A butcher-bird.

glossary.en: si zhong, suo ji - grasshopper, katydid
glossary.note: Si zhong is a locust-like insect and suo ji is a katydid; both are insects.
A cellar for storing ice.

qiyue.background: The Mao Preface says it tells how Hou Ji and the early dukes civilised the people, and how Duke of Zhou, hit by upheaval, set out the hardship of the royal enterprise; Zhu Xi said the Duke of Zhou was recalling how the earlier dukes taught farming and silk. Bin was where the Zhou people first lived. Two calendars are used in the poem: months called 'seventh' and 'ninth' follow the Xia calendar and the 'first days' and 'second days' follow the Zhou calendar, a favourite of scholars of ancient farming times.

chixiao.summary: A poem of the Bin Airs spoken by a small bird that has lost its young and worked hard on its nest. It accuses the owl of wrecking the nest and taking its chicks, and tells how hard it is to build a nest and how dangerous its position is. It is a comparison throughout, with a bitter and urgent tone.
chixiao.translation:
Owl, owl, you have taken my young - do not destroy my nest!
I loved them and toiled for them; raising my young brought me grief.
Before the sky clouded with rain, I took bark from the mulberry roots,
and bound my window and door tight.
Now, you people below - does any dare insult me?
My claws are worn and sore from gathering the reed-flower;
what I store up, I gather till my beak is worn out.
Still, I say, I have no home.
My feathers are thin and frayed, my tail ragged.
My nest is perched high, tossed about by wind and rain.
And I can only cry out in alarm.

glossary.note: An owl, here standing for the wicked person who harms the small bird.

glossary.en: en si qin si - loved and toiled
glossary.note: En is love, qin is toil, si is a particle.

glossary.en: yu zi zhi min si - the grief of raising young
glossary.note: Yu is to bring up; min is trouble and distress.
While there is still time.
To take, to strip.
The bark of mulberry roots.
To wind round and tie closely.

glossary.en: jie ju - worn and sore from toil (hands and claws)
glossary.note: Hands or claws stiff from overwork.

chixiao.background: According to the Book of Documents and the Mao Preface, the Duke of Zhou wrote this when King Cheng doubted him, to show his heart and the hardship of putting down the eastern rebellion and guarding the Zhou house. Later critics disagree, but most commentators still call it the Duke's. Today it can also be read simply as a fable told by a bird.

dongshan.summary: A poem of the Bin Airs of a soldier returning from the eastern campaign. In the drizzle he imagines his home overgrown and his wife missing him, and he remembers the joy of his wedding. Four stanzas open with the same couplet 「我徂東山，慆慆不歸，我來自東，零雨其濛」 ("I went to the Eastern Hills and for long did not return; now I come from the east in a fine drizzle"); it is sorrowful but not bitter, and shows the human side of war in fine detail.
dongshan.translation:
I went to the Eastern Hills, and for long did not return.
Now I come from the east, in a fine drizzle.
When I said in the east that I would go home, my heart in the west grieved.
I made those everyday clothes, no more to march with a gag in the mouth.
The wriggling caterpillars are there in the mulberry fields.
I curled up alone, sleeping beneath the cart.
I went to the Eastern Hills, and for long did not return.
Now I come from the east, in a fine drizzle.
The fruit of the snake-gourd creeps over the eaves.
Woodlice are in the room, long-legged spiders at the door.
The fields are trampled into deer-yards, fireflies glitter at night.
It is nothing to fear; it is something to long for.
I went to the Eastern Hills, and for long did not return.
Now I come from the east, in a fine drizzle.
The crane calls from the anthill, the wife sighs in the room.
She sprinkles and sweeps and stops the holes; my march is almost done.
The round bitter gourds lie on the chestnut firewood.
Since I saw them last, it is now three years.
I went to the Eastern Hills, and for long did not return.
Now I come from the east, in a fine drizzle.
The orioles fly, their wings gleaming.
That girl went to be married, the horses were bay and white.
Her mother tied her sash; the ceremonies were many.
The new bride was very fair; and the old one - how is she now?

glossary.note: To go off.
The look of a long stretch of time.
A thin, light rain.

glossary.en: wu shi xing mei - no more to march with a gag
glossary.note: Shi is 'affairs'; xing mei is the stick soldiers held in the mouth on the march to keep silent.
A trailing plant, Chinese cucumber.

glossary.en: yi wei, xiao shao - woodlouse, long-legged spider
glossary.note: Two small creatures found in empty houses.

glossary.en: yi yao xiao xing - fireflies glitter at night
glossary.note: Fireflies light up in the dark.

glossary.en: jiu shi qi yi - ninety and ten ceremonies
glossary.note: Many rites and rules.

dongshan.background: The Mao Preface says it was written when the Duke of Zhou returned from the eastern campaign after three years, and a grandee praised him; Zhu Xi said the soldiers returning were comforted. Today most take it as the words of a soldier returning home. Its detailed picture of the desolation after war and care for the family makes it a leading anti-war and homesick poem in the Songs.

fake.summary: A poem of the Bin Airs in which the need for an axe to cut an axe-handle is a comparison for the need of a matchmaker in taking a wife, the point being that things should follow their rule. A short poem in the manner of a maxim.
fake.translation:
How does one cut an axe-handle? Without an axe it cannot be done.
How does one take a wife? Without a matchmaker it cannot be done.
Cutting a handle, cutting a handle - the pattern is not far off.
When I meet that girl, the dishes are set out in rows.

glossary.note: The shaft of an axe.
Able, to manage.
Not, none.
A model; the old handle serves as the pattern for the new one.
To meet, to see.
Vessels for sacrifices and feasts; a bian is of bamboo and a dou of wood.
Laid out in neat rows.

fake.background: The Mao Preface says it praises the Duke of Zhou, and that a Zhou grandee mocked the court for not knowing him; Zhu Xi took a similar view. Today it is often read as a wedding song or a folk poem on the need for a matchmaker. 'Fa ke' later became a name for a matchmaker.

luming.summary: The first poem of the Lesser Odes, in the 'Odes' division, a banquet song in which a king or noble entertains his guests. Starting with deer calling their fellows to share wild plants, it tells of music, gifts, wine and joy, and of hope for guidance from the guests. Later banquets often used it, and Cao Cao quoted it in his Short Song.
luming.translation:
Yo-yo the deer cry, as they eat the wild mugwort.
I have honoured guests; we play the zither and blow the pipes.
We blow the pipes and play the reeds, and bring baskets of gifts.
Those who are kind to me show me the great way.
Yo-yo the deer cry, as they eat the wild southernwood.
I have honoured guests, whose fine words shine bright.
They set the people an example against meanness; the gentleman takes it as a pattern and follows it.
I have good wine; honoured guests feast and make merry.
Yo-yo the deer cry, as they eat the wild reed.
I have honoured guests; we play the zither and the lute.
We play the zither and lute, in harmony and deep joy.
I have good wine, to feast and delight the hearts of my guests.

glossary.en: you you - the cry of deer
glossary.note: The sound deer make.
A plant of the mugwort kind.

glossary.en: cheng kuang shi jiang - to bring baskets of gifts
glossary.note: To carry baskets holding gifts such as silk and present them; jiang is to offer.
A highway; it stands for the highest principle.

glossary.en: de yin kong zhao - fine words are very bright
glossary.note: De yin is good words and deeds; kong zhao means very clear.

glossary.en: shi min bu tiao - to show the people not to be shallow
glossary.note: To set the people an example against flippancy and meanness; shi is the same as another word for 'show'.
The same as the word for a feast.
Happy, in deep pleasure.

luming.background: The Mao Preface says it is for feasting the ministers and fine guests; Zhu Xi took it as a song for banquets in general. Today it is read as a noble's banquet song, possibly linked with rites of sacrifice and guest entertainment. Cao Cao's Short Song uses 「呦呦鹿鳴，食野之苹」 ("yo-yo the deer cry, as they eat the wild mugwort") to express his thirst for talent.

simu.summary: A poem of the Lesser Odes about an official on a long mission who longs for his parents but cannot go home because the king's business is endless, so he writes a song of longing. The refrain 'the king's work never ends' says that he is not his own master, and the clash of loyalty and filial duty is plain.
simu.translation:
The four stallions press on, the Zhou road winds on and on.
How could I not long to go home?
The king's work never ends; my heart is sore.
The four stallions press on, black-maned white horses panting.
How could I not long to go home?
The king's work never ends; I have no time to sit and rest.
The doves flutter, now flying, now landing, settling on a clump of oak.
The king's work never ends; I have no time to tend my father.
The doves flutter, now flying, now stopping, settling on a clump of wolfberry.
The king's work never ends; I have no time to tend my mother.
I drive those four black-maned white horses, galloping on and on.
How could I not long to go home?
So I make this song, to tell my longing for my mother.

glossary.note: Horses running without a stop.

glossary.en: wei yi - winding and distant (pronounced wei yi)
glossary.note: The road is curved and far.

glossary.en: wang shi mi gu - the king's work never stops
glossary.note: Mi gu means 'without cease'; gu is to rest.
The breathing of horses.

glossary.en: qi chu - to sit and rest
glossary.note: Qi is to kneel and sit; chu is to dwell.
A pigeon-like bird.
To look after one's parents.
To think of; another reading is 'to tell'.

simu.background: The Mao Preface says it is for consoling a returned envoy, a song of the king rewarding a minister back from a mission; Zhu Xi also called it music for comforting an envoy. Today most read it as the words of an official on service. The theme of loyalty and filial duty that cannot both be met is often quoted later.

huanghuangzhehua.summary: A poem of the Lesser Odes sung to send off or encourage an envoy. It shows the envoy rushing over the plains and low ground, working hard and asking for advice everywhere in order to finish his mission, and reflects the Zhou habit of seeking counsel and acting with care.
huanghuangzhehua.translation:
Bright shine the flowers on the plains and low ground.
The envoys press on in crowds, always fearing they do not measure up.
My horses are young, the six reins smooth as if moist.
Galloping, driving, I go all round asking for counsel.
My horses are grey-black dappled, the six reins like silk.
Galloping, driving, I go all round asking for plans.
My horses are black-maned white, the six reins glossy.
Galloping, driving, I go all round asking for judgement.
My horses are dapple grey, the six reins evenly drawn.
Galloping, driving, I go all round asking for advice.

glossary.en: huang huang zhe hua - bright flowers
glossary.note: Huang huang is bright and clear; hua is the same as 'flower'.

glossary.en: shen shen - hurrying in crowds (pronounced shen)
glossary.note: The look of many people on the move.

glossary.en: mei huai mi ji - always fearing one falls short
glossary.note: Constantly worried one is not up to it.

glossary.en: liu pei ru ru - the six reins smooth as if moist
glossary.note: Four horses have six reins in all; the reins are soft as though wet.

glossary.en: qi, luo, yin - three horse colours
glossary.note: Qi is dark-blue-grey striped; luo is a white horse with a black mane; yin is a mixed black-and-white grey.

glossary.en: zhou yuan zi zou - going about asking
glossary.note: Zhou means all round; yuan is 'then'; zi zou is to consult.

glossary.en: zi mou, zi duo, zi xun - consult, weigh, ask
glossary.note: To plan together, to consider, to enquire: all close in sense.

huanghuangzhehua.background: The Mao Preface says it is the king sending an envoy and giving him guidance; Zhu Xi also called it music for sending an envoy. Later 'huang hua' often means an envoy or being sent on a mission.

changdi.summary: A poem of the Lesser Odes in praise of brotherhood. The close-set flowers of the cherry-plum open it. It says brothers are the best support in death, trouble and distress, yet in peace they are easily replaced by friends, and ends in the joy of feasting and a united household. The argument is clear, joining reasoning with feeling.
changdi.translation:
The flowers of the cherry-plum, how their calyxes glow!
Of all the people today, none are like brothers.
At the dread of death and loss, brothers feel deeply.
When bodies lie heaped on the plain, brothers come looking.
The wagtail is on the plain; brothers help in trouble.
Though one has good friends, they can only sigh long.
Brothers may quarrel inside the wall, but facing outward they fend off insult.
Though one has good friends, in the long run they give no help.
When death and disorder are over, and all is calm and at peace,
even with brothers, one prefers friends.
Set out your dishes, and drink wine to the full.
With brothers all together, in harmony and joy, close as children.
Wife and children in good accord, like zither and lute.
With brothers united, joy and harmony run deep.
May your household be at peace, and your wife and children happy.
Think it through, consider it - is it not truly so?

glossary.note: A small tree whose flowers grow in clusters.

glossary.en: e bu wei wei - calyxes so bright
glossary.note: E is the same as the calyx; bu is a particle; wei wei is bright and glowing.
Kong is 'very'.
A small water bird that calls when in trouble, often used to stand for brothers.
To squabble.

glossary.en: wai yu qi wu - to fend off insult from outside
glossary.note: Wu is the same as 'insult'.

glossary.en: zheng ye wu rong - in the long run no help
glossary.note: Zheng is long; rong is help.
Friends.

changdi.background: The Mao Preface says it is a banquet for brothers, and elsewhere that the Duke of Zhou wrote it when Guan Shu and Cai Shu went astray; Zhu Xi also called it a feast song for brothers. Because of the line 「兄弟鬩于牆，外禦其務」 ("brothers may quarrel inside the wall, but facing outward they fend off insult"), later words such as 'quarrel within the wall' and 'hands and feet' mean brothers.

famu.summary: A poem of the Lesser Odes for a feast of friends and kin. Birds calling for friends as men chop wood lead into the thought that people should seek friends too. It goes on to the food and wine prepared for elders, uncles and brothers, adds that quarrels over small things should be avoided, and ends in drumming and dancing, stressing friendship.
famu.translation:
Ding-ding we fell the trees; the birds sing ying-ying.
They come out from the deep valley and move to the tall trees.
Calling ying-ying, they seek the voice of a friend.
Look at those birds - even they seek a friend's voice.
How much more should a person - not seek friends?
The spirits listen, and in the end give peace and harmony.
Hu-hu we fell the trees; the strained wine is fine.
With plump young lambs, we invite the uncles.
Better they should happen not to come than that I should neglect them.
Bright, swept and sprinkled, I set out eight bowls of food.
With plump rams, we invite the uncles on my mother's side.
Better they should happen not to come than that I should be at fault.
We fell trees on the slope; the strained wine is plentiful,
dishes set in rows; let no brother be far away.
People lose their good feeling over a bit of dried rations.
If there is wine, strain it for me; if not, buy it for me.
Kan-kan beat the drum for me, dun-dun dance for me.
While I have leisure, drink this clear wine!

glossary.en: zheng zheng - the sound of chopping
glossary.note: The noise of felling trees.

glossary.en: ying ying - the sound of birds calling to each other
glossary.note: The mutual calls of birds.
All the more so.
To clear the wine.
A young sheep.

glossary.en: zhu fu, zhu jiu - paternal elders, maternal uncles
glossary.note: Zhu fu are older men of the same surname; zhu jiu are relatives of other surnames.

glossary.en: gan hou yi qian - falling out over dried rations
glossary.note: To quarrel or fail in courtesy over trifling food.

glossary.en: xu, gu - clear wine, to buy wine
glossary.note: Xu is strained wine; gu is to buy wine.

famu.background: The Mao Preface says it is a feast for friends and old acquaintances; Zhu Xi called it a feast song for friends and old friends. The line 「嚶其鳴矣，求其友聲」 ("calling ying-ying, they seek the voice of a friend") became famous for seeking friends and like minds, and 'ying ming' means friends who respond to each other.

caiwei.summary: A poem of the Lesser Odes sung by a frontier soldier on his way home. The first part tells the hardship of the posting and homesickness; the middle gives the urgency of war and the order of the army; the end sets a sad scene against sad feeling in 「昔我往矣，楊柳依依。今我來思，雨雪霏霏」 ("when I left, the willows drooped soft and green; now I come back, rain and snow fall thick"), long counted among the most moving lines of the Songs.
caiwei.translation:
We pick the vetch, we pick the vetch, the vetch is just shooting up.
We say "go home, go home", but the year is ending.
No house, no home - because of the Xianyun.
No time to sit and rest - because of the Xianyun.
We pick the vetch, we pick the vetch, the vetch is tender.
We say "go home, go home", and our hearts are troubled.
My grieving heart burns; we are hungry and thirsty.
My post is not fixed; there is no envoy to send home with word.
We pick the vetch, we pick the vetch, the vetch is tough.
We say "go home, go home", but the year has reached the tenth month.
The king's work never ends; there is no time to sit and rest.
My heart is sorely pained; my march has no return.
What is that so bright? It is the flower of the cherry-plum.
What is that great carriage? It is the commander's chariot.
The war chariots are yoked, the four stallions are tall and strong.
How dare we settle? Three victories in a month.
I yoke those four stallions, the four stallions are vigorous.
The commander rides on them, the soldiers are screened by them.
The four stallions are orderly; ivory-tipped bows, fish-skin quivers.
How could we not be on guard daily? The Xianyun are very pressing!
When I left, the willows drooped soft and green.
Now I come back, rain and snow fall thick.
I walk the road slowly, thirsty and hungry.
My heart is sore with sorrow, and none knows my grief!

glossary.note: Sprouts of wild vetch, edible, picked often by men on campaign.
A nomadic people of the north in Zhou times.

glossary.en: qi ju - to sit and rest
glossary.note: To settle and sit down.
The look of a heart burning with worry.

glossary.en: mi shi gui pin - no envoy to go home and ask after them
glossary.note: No messenger who can go home to give greetings.
The ancients called the tenth month 'the yang month'.

glossary.en: xiang mi yu fu - ivory-tipped bow, fish-skin quiver
glossary.note: A bow trimmed with ivory and a quiver of fish skin.

glossary.en: yang liu yi yi - willows drooping
glossary.note: Yi yi means soft and drooping, with the feeling of clinging.

caiwei.background: The Mao Preface says it was for sending off troops: in King Wen's time there was the threat of the Kunyi on the west and the Xianyun on the north, and the king sent men to guard the central lands; Zhu Xi said it was written by soldiers on garrison duty. Today it is mostly read as the song of a soldier coming home, and shows the suffering war brings an individual, one of the best-known war poems in the Songs.

chuche.summary: A poem of the Lesser Odes about the general Nan Zhong of King Xuan of Zhou, who campaigned against the Xianyun, built a wall at Shuofang and came home victorious. It also shows the hardships and homesickness of the troops. The early stanzas describe the march; later ones turn to homesickness and victory, with a stately army and fine feeling, the tone moving from strain to triumph.
chuche.translation:
I bring out my chariot, to the pasture there.
From the place of the Son of Heaven, I was told to come.
I call the drivers and tell them to load up.
The king's work is full of difficulty; it is urgent.
I bring out my chariot to the outskirts.
I set up the tortoise-and-snake banners and raise the yak-tail banners.
Those falcon and snake banners - why do they not flutter?
My heart is sore, and the drivers are worn out.
The king ordered Nan Zhong to go and build a wall at Fang.
The chariots roll out, peng-peng; the banners are bright.
The Son of Heaven commands me to wall that northern place.
Mighty Nan Zhong has swept away the Xianyun.
When I left, the millet and sorghum were in flower.
Now I return, rain and snow cover the road.
The king's work is full of difficulty; there is no time to sit and rest.
How could I not long to go home? I fear this written order.
Yao-yao chirp the grass insects, ti-ti leap the grasshoppers.
I have not seen my lord; my heart is full of worry.
Once I have seen my lord, my heart will settle.
Mighty Nan Zhong has struck the western Rong.
The spring days are long, the grass and trees lush.
Orioles sing sweetly, and many gather the white mugwort.
Prisoners for questioning are taken; then we return home.
Mighty Nan Zhong has levelled the Xianyun.

glossary.note: Grazing land in the outskirts.

glossary.en: zhao, mao - the tortoise-and-snake banner, the yak-tail banner
glossary.note: Zhao is a banner painted with a tortoise and snake; mao is a banner trimmed with yak tail.
A flag painted with a falcon or hawk.
The north, meaning the frontier.
A general of King Xuan of Zhou, said to have campaigned against the Xianyun and the western Rong.
A written order or document on bamboo slips, here a military order.

glossary.en: yao yao cao chong, ti ti fu zhong - chirping insects, leaping grasshoppers
glossary.note: The same lines as 'Grass Insects' in the Shaonan; the insects open a song of longing.

glossary.en: zhi xun huo chou - to take captives for questioning
glossary.note: To seize enemy prisoners to be interrogated.

chuche.background: The Mao Preface says it comforts a returned general, a song of consoling the commander of a returning army; Zhu Xi said it records the troops going out and coming back. The poem names the general Nan Zhong, and has long been used as source material for Western Zhou military affairs and borders. Some modern scholars think its author was a junior officer on the campaign.

didu.summary: A poem of the Lesser Odes, in the voice of a wife whose husband is on service. When the pear tree bears fruit and its leaves thicken, she longs for him, worries, consults the diviners, and tells herself he must be close. Three stanzas move along with the changing seasons to show time passing, with honest feeling.
didu.translation:
A lone pear tree stands, its fruit round and plump.
The king's work never ends; day after day it goes on.
It is the tenth month; your heart is sore; the soldier may have leisure.
A lone pear tree stands, its leaves lush.
The king's work never ends; my heart is sore with grief.
The plants are lush; your heart is sad; the soldier will return.
I climb that northern hill and pick wolfberries.
The king's work never ends, and my parents worry.
Sandalwood carts are shabby, the four stallions weary; the soldier is not far.
If he has not loaded up and come, my heart is sorely pained.
The date has passed and he has not come; I am full of worry.
Tortoise and stalks both agree; they say he is near; the soldier is close.

glossary.note: The look of a tree standing by itself.
The wild pear tree.
The look of round, full fruit.

glossary.en: wang shi mi gu - the king's work never ends
glossary.note: The king's tasks have no pause.
The yang month is the tenth month; zhi is a particle.

glossary.en: tan che chan chan - sandalwood cart, shabby
glossary.note: A service cart made of sandalwood, worn and old.
Tired out.

glossary.en: bu shi xie zhi - both divinations agree
glossary.note: Both divination by tortoise shell and by stalks give the same answer.

didu.background: The Mao Preface says it comforts men back from service; Zhu Xi called it music for consoling troops come home. Today most read it as a poem of a woman at home; the details of 'the date has passed' and 'both divinations agree' show the anxiety of waiting and the effort to comfort oneself.

yuli.summary: A poem of the Lesser Odes praising good wine and plentiful fish at a feast. The first three stanzas begin with fish swimming into a trap, listing the fish and the rich wine; the last three sum up the abundance, the good taste and the full range, a banquet song celebrating a good year.
yuli.translation:
The fish swim into the trap: yellow-cheek fish and sand minnows.
Our host has wine, delicious and plentiful.
The fish swim into the trap: bream and snakehead.
Our host has wine, plentiful and delicious.
The fish swim into the trap: catfish and carp.
Our host has wine, delicious and abundant.
The goods are many, and they are fine.
The goods are tasty, and they are complete.
The goods are abundant, and they are in season.

glossary.en: yu li yu liu - fish enter the trap
glossary.note: Li is the same as a word for 'fall into'; liu is a bamboo fish trap.

glossary.en: chang, sha - yellow-cheek fish, sand minnow
glossary.note: Chang is the yellow-cheek fish; sha is a small fish.
Fang is bream; li is the snakehead.
Yan is a catfish; li is the carp.
Delicious.
Plentiful and full.

glossary.en: wei qi jia yi - and they are fine
glossary.note: Wei is a particle; jia is good.

yuli.background: The Mao Preface says it praises the abundance of all things and their ability to provide for ritual; Zhu Xi said it was a general banquet song. The names of the fish show what Zhou people knew of water products. Today it is mostly seen as a feast song, and some say it was sung at the feast after a sacrifice.

nanyoujiayu.summary: A poem of the Lesser Odes for entertaining guests. Fine fish of the south in shoals open it and show the host's warmth; drooping trees hung with gourds and fluttering doves suggest closeness between host and guests and joy that does not end.
nanyoujiayu.translation:
In the south are fine fish, swimming in shoals.
Our host has wine; honoured guests feast and are glad.
In the south are fine fish, swarming in shoals.
Our host has wine; honoured guests feast and enjoy themselves.
In the south stands a drooping tree, with sweet gourds trailing over it.
Our host has wine; honoured guests feast and are set at ease.
The doves flutter, coming in flocks.
Our host has wine; honoured guests feast and think of coming again.

glossary.note: Fish that taste good.
Many together; zheng is 'many'.
Fish moving about; one view takes it as fishing with a cover-net.
Fish moving about; one view takes it as fishing with a small net.

glossary.en: shi yan yi le - feast and be glad
glossary.note: Shi is a particle; yan is the same as 'feast'.
Happy.
A gourd with a sweet taste.

glossary.en: you si - to think of coming again
glossary.note: To think again, here urging guests to return.

nanyoujiayu.background: The Mao Preface says it takes pleasure in sharing with the worthy: in a peaceful age the lord had wine and food and enjoyed sharing it; Zhu Xi said it was a general feast song. Today it is mostly seen as a banquet song for guests, with fish, gourds and doves as images of harmony between host and guests.

liaoxiao.summary: A poem of the Lesser Odes sung when the Son of Heaven feasts the lords or the lords come to court. Tall mugwort heavy with dew opens it, standing for the favour a lord receives; four stanzas rise from the joy of meeting, to honour, to ease, to a splendid train. It praises the lord, using evocation.
liaoxiao.translation:
Tall stands the fragrant mugwort, heavy with falling dew.
Now I have seen my lord, my heart is eased.
We feast, laugh and talk, and so are held in good repute.
Tall stands the fragrant mugwort, with dew thick upon it.
Now I have seen my lord, I am favoured and honoured.
His virtue does not falter; long life and never forgotten.
Tall stands the fragrant mugwort, with dew soaking it.
Now I have seen my lord, he is at ease, kind and gentle.
A good elder brother and a good younger brother; fine in virtue, long-lived and happy.
Tall stands the fragrant mugwort, with dew rich upon it.
Now I have seen my lord, the leather bridles jingle.
The harmony and luan bells ring sweetly, and all blessings gather.

glossary.note: The look of a tall plant.
A fragrant artemisia used in ancient sacrifices.
A lot of dew.
Here, to feel at ease.

glossary.en: wei long wei guang - honoured and glorious
glossary.note: Long is the same as a word for 'favour'; the line means favour and glory.

glossary.en: kai ti - kind and easy-going (pronounced kai ti)
glossary.note: Cheerful and gentle.
The harness of a horse, made of leather.
Bells on a carriage: he on the crossbar at the front and luan on the yoke.

liaoxiao.background: The Mao Preface says the king's kindness reached everywhere within the four seas; Zhu Xi said the lords came to court and the Son of Heaven feasted and sang this to them. Most today read it as a banquet poem of the king or a noble; the mugwort and dew are a common evocative image.

zhanlu.summary: A poem of the Lesser Odes for the Son of Heaven's night banquet for the lords. The dew that dries only in sun opens it, to say that no one leaves the night's drinking sober; wolfberry, thorn, tung and catalpa stand for the lords' virtue and bearing. The tone is solemn and cheerful, in evocation and comparison.
zhanlu.translation:
Heavy lies the dew; without the sun it will not dry.
Peacefully we drink through the night; none go home until drunk.
Heavy lies the dew on the lush grass.
Peacefully we drink at night in the clan hall, and complete it.
Heavy lies the dew on the wolfberry and thorn.
Bright and sincere are the lords, all of fine virtue.
The tung and the catalpa, their fruit hanging down.
Kind and easy-going lords, all of fine bearing.

glossary.note: The look of thick dew.

glossary.en: fei yang bu xi - without the sun it will not dry
glossary.note: Xi means dry.

glossary.en: yan yan ye yin - drinking peacefully at night
glossary.note: Yan yan is quiet and happy.
Kao means to bring to completion.
Radiant and trustworthy.
Good character.
Two kinds of deciduous tree.
The look of drooping fruit.

zhanlu.background: The Mao Preface says it is the Son of Heaven feasting the lords; Zhu Xi said the same. The words 'none go home until drunk' later became a common toast. The dew is a figure for the king's favour, which only the sun (the king's majesty) can dry.

baiju.summary: A poem of the Lesser Odes to keep a worthy man from leaving. Using the white colt eating sprouts in the yard as an excuse, it wishes to tether the guest's horse and prolong the visit; he rides off all the same to hide in an empty valley. The last lines beg him not to be stingy with news or grow distant. The tone is earnest and sad.
baiju.translation:
A bright white colt eats the sprouts in my yard.
Hobble him, tether him, to lengthen this morning.
The one I speak of, let him stroll here at ease.
A bright white colt eats the bean leaves in my yard.
Hobble him, tether him, to lengthen this evening.
The one I speak of, let him be an honoured guest here.
The bright white colt comes splendidly.
Be you duke, be you marquis, may your ease have no end.
Be careful of your leisure; hold back your thoughts of withdrawing.
The bright white colt is in the empty valley, with a bundle of fresh fodder.
The man is like jade; do not make your words as rare as gold and jade,
and do not keep a distant heart.

glossary.note: Clean and shining.

glossary.en: zhi, wei - to hobble, to tether
glossary.note: Zhi is to bind the legs; wei is to tie by the neck.
The worthy man.
In this place.
The leaves of beans, eaten as a vegetable.
The wish to hide away.

glossary.en: sheng chu yi shu - a bundle of fresh fodder
glossary.note: A bunch of green grass for the horse, also standing for a simple hermit's life.
A heart that has grown far off.

baiju.background: The Mao Preface says a grandee criticised King Xuan for not keeping worthy men; Zhu Xi said a worthy man had ridden off on a white colt, so the poem tries to keep him. Today it is mostly read as a poem of seeing off or detaining a hermit. The phrase 'a white colt passing a crack' comes from the Zhuangzi and has nothing to do with this poem.

woxingqiye.summary: A poem of the Lesser Odes, the complaint of a woman cast off by her husband. She went to live with him because of the marriage but he would not take her in; in the end she understands that it is not for money but because he has a new love. The tone is aggrieved but restrained, short and strong.
woxingqiye.translation:
I walk in the wilds, where the stinking ailanthus stands thick.
For the sake of our marriage, I come to live with you.
You do not keep me, so I go back to my own land.
I walk in the wilds and pick the sorrel.
For the sake of our marriage, I come to lodge with you.
You do not keep me, so I go home again.
I walk in the wilds and pick the wild turnip.
You do not think of the old tie, but seek a new mate.
It is not for wealth, but only for novelty.

glossary.note: Leafy and lush.
A tree with poor wood.
Hun is the same as 'marriage'.

glossary.en: xu - to keep, to take in
glossary.note: To support or hold.
A wild vegetable.
A wild root vegetable.
Te means a partner.
Merely.

woxingqiye.background: The Mao Preface says it mocks King Xuan: in that time men and women lost the right way and marriage had no good faith; Zhu Xi said someone moved to another state to rely on her marriage but was not taken in, so she wrote this. Today it is read as a poem of an abandoned woman or of someone who found no shelter. The last two lines have always been explained in several ways.

sigan.summary: A poem of the Lesser Odes in blessing for a new palace. It first describes the building by hill and stream, then the comfort of the rooms, then wishes for sons and daughters in the form of dream interpretation, and teaches the proper role of daughters. It is important evidence on Zhou building and life.
sigan.translation:
Smooth flows the stream, deep and dim lies the southern hill.
Like bamboo in clumps, like pines in luxuriance.
Brothers, be good to one another, and do not scheme against one another.
To carry on the line of ancestors, we build a hundred walls.
The doors face southwest; here we live, here we stay, here we laugh and talk.
We bind the frames, ge-ge; we pound the earth, tuo-tuo.
Wind and rain are kept out, birds and rats are gone, and the lord finds shelter.
Like a man standing on tiptoe in reverence, sharp as an arrow,
the roof is like a bird spreading its wings, the eaves like a pheasant taking flight.
The lord ascends.
The courtyard is level, the pillars tall and straight.
The bright rooms are spacious, the dark ones deep and quiet.
The lord is at ease.
Rush mats below, bamboo mats above; here he sleeps in peace.
He sleeps, he wakes, and asks about his dream.
What is the lucky dream? Bears and brown bears, vipers and snakes.
The diviner interprets it:
bears and brown bears are the omen for sons;
vipers and snakes are the omen for daughters.
If a son is born, he will sleep on a bed,
be dressed in robes, and play with a jade sceptre.
His cry will be loud, his red knee-covering splendid, a lord of house and state.
If a daughter is born, she will sleep on the floor,
be wrapped in a plain wrap, and play with a spindle-whorl.
She should do no wrong and no good; only consider wine and food,
and bring no trouble to her parents.

glossary.note: Water running smoothly.
A ravine stream; si gan is this stream.
Dense and thick.

glossary.en: si xu bi zu - to carry on the line of forebears
glossary.note: Si is the same as a word for 'to succeed'.

glossary.en: ru qi si yi - like a man standing on tiptoe
glossary.note: Respectful and upright, like someone on tiptoe.

glossary.en: ru niao si ge, ru hui si fei - like a bird's wings, like a pheasant in flight
glossary.note: The roof spreads like wings and the eaves soar like a pheasant.
A jade piece given to a boy to play with, showing the hope that he will become a great man.
A pottery whorl given to a girl, standing for the weaving she will do.

sigan.background: The Mao Preface says King Xuan was inspecting his new house; Zhu Xi said the palace was finished and a feast was held with a song to mark it. Most take this view today. The different hopes for boys and girls show Zhou ideas of gender, and 'play with a sceptre' and 'play with a tile' later became expressions for the birth of a boy or girl.

wuyang.summary: A poem of the Lesser Odes about flourishing herds of sheep and cattle and a herdsman's dream. First come flocks and herds and the herdsmen in straw capes and bamboo hats, then the herdsman dreams of fish and banners, which the diviner reads as a good harvest and growing families. It is lively and has the tone of a blessing.
wuyang.translation:
Who says you have no sheep? Three hundred in a flock.
Who says you have no cattle? Ninety black-lipped yellow oxen.
Your sheep come, their horns bunched together;
your cattle come, their ears flicking.
Some come down the slope, some drink at the pond.
Some lie down, some stir; your herdsmen come.
With straw capes and bamboo hats, some carrying their rations.
Thirty colours - your livestock are complete.
Your herdsmen come with firewood, thick and thin.
With females and males, your sheep come.
Firm and careful, none lags, none breaks away.
He waves with his arm, and all come and go up.
The herdsman dreams: many fish.
Tortoise-snake banners turning to falcon banners; the diviner interprets.
Many fish - a bountiful year.
Tortoise-snake banners turning to falcon banners - households will teem.

glossary.note: A yellow ox with a black muzzle.
The look of horns close together.
Ears wet and moving; another view says the ears move as the cow chews the cud.
To move about.

glossary.en: he suo he li - in straw capes and bamboo hats
glossary.note: He is the same as a word for 'carry'; wearing a rain cape and hat.

glossary.en: san shi wei wu - thirty colours
glossary.note: Livestock of thirty coat colours, meaning all kinds present.

glossary.en: zhao wei yu yi - the tortoise banner becomes a falcon banner
glossary.note: A dream sign.
Many and prosperous.

wuyang.background: The Mao Preface says King Xuan was examining the herdsmen, that is, checking on herding in his time so that it flourished; Zhu Xi said it is a herdsman's poem. The dream interpretation reflects the Zhou habit of reading dreams for good and bad luck, and shows the prosperity of herding at that time.

qiaoyan.summary: A poem of the Lesser Odes satirising slander that ruins government. The author calls on Heaven, says the disorder began with a king who believed slander, and attacks flatterers with 「巧言如簧，顏之厚矣」 ("clever words like a reed organ - how thick the face is!"). The tone is angry and the argument sharp.
qiaoyan.translation:
O far, vast Heaven, I call you father and mother.
I have no guilt, no blame, yet such confusion is so great.
Heaven is very terrible; I am truly guiltless.
Heaven is vast and great; I am truly blameless.
When the disorder first arose, the first untruth was tolerated.
When disorder arose again, the lord believed slander.
If the lord were angry, disorder would quickly be checked.
If the lord were glad of good, disorder would quickly end.
The lord swears oath after oath, and so disorder grows.
The lord trusts thieves, and so disorder turns savage.
Thieves' words are very sweet, and so disorder spreads.
They do not do their duty; they are the king's sickness.
The great ancestral halls were built by the lords.
The orderly grand plans were fixed by the sages.
Other men have hearts, and I can fathom them.
The leaping cunning hare meets a dog and is caught.
The soft, supple trees were planted by the lords.
Words that come and go on the road, my heart counts them over.
Smooth, grand talk comes out of the mouth.
Clever words like a reed organ - how thick the face is!
Who is that man? He lives on the river bank.
He has no strength, no courage, yet he is the stairway to disorder.
With his sore shins and swollen feet, what courage does he have?
His schemes are many; how many are the followers in his house?

glossary.note: The wide heavens.

glossary.en: yue fu mu qie - calling Heaven father and mother
glossary.note: Qie is a particle.

glossary.en: jian shi ji han - the first untruth was tolerated
glossary.note: Jian is not trusting, han is to hold; the king at first did not trust, but let the slander in.

glossary.en: dao yan kong gan - thieves' words are very sweet
glossary.note: Slander is exceedingly pleasing to hear; dao yan is slander.

glossary.en: zhi zhi da you - the orderly grand plan
glossary.note: You means plan or policy.
A sly rabbit.

glossary.en: qiao yan ru huang - clever words like a reed
glossary.note: Smooth talk as pleasant as the sound of a reed in a mouth organ.
A disease with swollen legs.

qiaoyan.background: The Mao Preface says it mocks King You: a grandee, hurt by slander, wrote this poem; Zhu Xi said it was by a man who was slandered. Most take this view today. The words 'clever words like a reed' and 'clever words and fine looks' later became sayings against smooth talkers.

liaoe.summary: A poem of the Lesser Odes, a lament of a dutiful son who longs for his parents and grieves that he cannot care for them. Tall e-herb that turns out to be wormwood stands for his failure to repay them. The passage 「父兮生我，母兮鞠我」 ("father begot me, mother raised me") uses nine verbs to tell all a parent's kindness, and has been recited ever since.
liaoe.translation:
Tall and tall the e-herb - it is not e, but wormwood.
Alas, my parents, who bore me with toil.
Tall and tall the e-herb - it is not e, but mugwort.
Alas, my parents, who bore me through weariness.
The small jar is empty - it is the shame of the large vat.
The life of a lonely one - better to have died long ago.
Without a father, whom to lean on? Without a mother, whom to trust?
Going out, I carry sorrow; coming in, I have no one to go to.
Father begot me, mother raised me;
they stroked me, nourished me, brought me up, taught me,
looked after me, watched over me again and again, held me in their arms wherever they went.
I wish to repay their kindness, but it is as vast as Heaven, without limit.
The southern hill is towering, the whirlwind rushes.
Everyone else is fortunate; why am I alone so afflicted?
The southern hill is high, the whirlwind roars.
Everyone else is fortunate; I alone cannot finish caring for them!

glossary.note: The look of a tall plant.
An edible wild plant; the poet says it is not e but wormwood, standing for himself as a worthless son.
Hard work.

glossary.en: ping zhi qing yi, wei lei zhi chi - the small jar is empty, the large vat's shame
glossary.note: A ping is a small wine bottle and a lei a big wine vessel; when the bottle is empty it shames the vat, meaning that the parents' suffering is the children's fault.
Xian means few: someone left helpless and alone.
To hold grief in the heart.
To bring up.

glossary.en: fu, xu, yu, gu, fu, fu - stroke, nourish, teach, look after, watch over, carry in arms
glossary.note: The six verbs, with the three before them, mean stroking, cherishing, rearing, caring for, watching again and again, and holding in arms.

liaoe.background: The Mao Preface says it mocks King You: the people suffered and a dutiful son could not care for his parents to the end; Zhu Xi said a dutiful son on service could not look after his parents. The Book of Jin records that Wang Pou wept on reading this poem, and later writers often use it for thoughts of parents. Today it is regarded as the most moving poem of filial longing.

dadong.summary: A poem of the Lesser Odes, a protest by the people of the eastern states against the heavy dues and unequal burdens laid on them by the Zhou royal house. The Zhou road is smooth while their goods are carried off; the westerners wear splendid clothes while the easterners' weaving is seized. The poet then uses stars, the Weaver Girl, the Ox-Herd, the Winnowing Basket and the Dipper, sighing that they have names but no use. The writing is striking and imaginative.
dadong.translation:
A bowl is heaped with food, a thorn-wood spoon curves.
The Zhou road is smooth as a whetstone, straight as an arrow.
The lords tread on it; the small folk watch.
Looking back at it, I weep, tears streaming.
In the lesser east and the greater east, the looms are empty.
Twisted kudzu sandals must tread the frost.
Those light-stepping lordlings walk the Zhou road.
They come and go, and my heart is sick.
Cold flows the spring from the side; do not soak the cut firewood.
Troubled, I sigh awake; alas for us weary folk.
Firewood once cut can still be carried;
we weary folk should also be allowed to rest.
The sons of the east work and are never comforted.
The sons of the west wear gorgeous clothes.
The sons of the boatmen wear bear furs.
The sons of the retainers are tried in all the offices.
Some have their wine; the east is not given even thin drink.
Gleaming jade pendants - yet not for any merit.
In the sky is the Han, the Milky Way, looking down and shining.
On tiptoe that Weaver Girl moves through seven stations all day.
Though seven stations, she weaves no finished pattern.
Bright is the Ox-Herd star, but it pulls no cart.
In the east is the Morning Star, in the west the Evening Star.
Curved is the Net of heaven, set up in a row.
In the south is the Winnowing Basket, but it cannot winnow.
In the north is the Dipper, but it cannot ladle wine.
In the south the Basket draws in its tongue.
In the north the Dipper lifts its handle to the west.

glossary.en: gui sun - bowl of food, cooked meal
glossary.note: A gui is a vessel for food; sun is cooked food.
A spoon made of thorn wood.

glossary.en: Zhou dao ru di - the Zhou road smooth as a whetstone
glossary.note: The highway to the Zhou capital; di is a whetstone, for flatness.

glossary.en: zhu zhou qi kong - looms empty
glossary.note: Zhu and zhou are parts of a loom; the cloth has all been taken.
Jaunty, strolling by oneself.

glossary.en: Zhi Nu, Qian Niu - Weaver Girl, Ox-Herd
glossary.note: Star names: the Weaver Girl is three stars, and the Ox-Herd, also called the Drum of the River, lies across the Milky Way from her.

glossary.en: Qi Ming, Chang Geng - Morning Star and Evening Star
glossary.note: Both are Venus: Qi Ming in the morning and Chang Geng in the evening.

glossary.en: ji, dou - the Winnowing Basket and the Dipper
glossary.note: The Basket in the south and the Dipper in the north are star groups shaped like a winnowing basket and a wine ladle, but cannot really be used.

dadong.background: The Mao Preface says a grandee of Tan wrote the poem to tell of his suffering: the east was worn out by service and drained of wealth. Zhu Xi also took it as the east's complaint of heavy duties for the Zhou king. By turning the Weaver Girl, Ox-Herd, Basket and Dipper into 'name without substance', the poem gives an early star lore that bears on the later Cowherd and Weaver Girl tale.

beishan.summary: A poem of the Lesser Odes, the complaint of a petty official forced to overwork. The first half shows him busy from morning to night for the king and anxious about his parents; the second half sets twelve 'some...' lines against each other, the ease of colleagues and his own toil, full of the sense of injustice. It is the Songs' foremost example of parallelism and contrast.

glossary.note: A plant whose fruit can be picked and eaten.
A strong build.

glossary.en: pu tian zhi xia, mo fei wang tu - under the broad sky, none is not the king's land
glossary.note: Pu is the same as 'broad': there is no land that is not the king's.

glossary.en: shuai tu zhi bin, mo fei wang chen - to the ends of the earth, none is not the king's servant
glossary.note: Following the land to its end, every person is the king's subject.
Uneven in sharing out.
Xian here means toil: the poet alone is made to work.

glossary.en: xian wo fang jiang - praised as in my prime
glossary.note: Xian is 'good' and jiang is 'strong'.
Busy with no spare moment.

beishan.background: The Mao Preface says a grandee criticised King You for unfair use of labour, so that the poet worked at his task and could not look after his parents; Zhu Xi said an official of a lesser state was worn out by the king's service. The line 「溥天之下，莫非王土」 ("under the broad sky, none is not the king's land") is the most widely quoted, and also an important source for the Zhou idea of royal power.

xiaowan.summary: A poem of the Lesser Odes, urging brothers and sons to behave carefully and not to drink to excess. The poet remembers his forebears, warns against drink and pleasure, teaches the young, and tells them to be respectful and careful. The ending, 「如臨深淵，如履薄冰」 ("as if standing at the edge of an abyss, as if treading on thin ice"), is often quoted and carries a deep sense.
xiaowan.translation:
The little cooing dove flies high up to the sky.
My heart is sad as I think of my forebears.
At daybreak I cannot sleep, thinking of my two parents.
Those of upright wisdom stay gentle and restrained when drinking.
The foolish know nothing; once drunk, they grow worse day by day.
Each of you, mind your bearing; Heaven's mandate does not come twice.
In the middle of the plain are beans, which common folk gather.
The mulberry caterpillar has young, and the wasp carries them off.
Teach your sons, that they may be good and like them.
Look at the wagtail, flying and calling.
Day by day I go on, and month by month you go on.
Rise early, sleep late, and do not shame those who bore you.
The bullfinch, jiao-jiao, pecks millet all over the threshing floor.
Alas, I am sick, poor and alone, and must face the court and the jail.
Grain in hand, I go out to divine - how can I be fortunate?
Gentle, courteous people are as if perched on a tree.
Fearful and careful, as if standing at a gorge.
Trembling and cautious, as if treading on thin ice.

glossary.note: A turtle-dove.

glossary.en: han fei li tian - to fly high up to the sky
glossary.note: Han fei is high flight; li is to reach.

glossary.en: ming fa bu mei - not sleeping at daybreak
glossary.note: Unable to sleep even when day dawns.
Meaning the parents.
Mild and able to control oneself.

glossary.en: ming ling you zi, guo luo fu zhi - the caterpillar's young, carried off by the wasp
glossary.note: The ancients wrongly thought the wasp took the caterpillar's young to raise as its own; it stands for adopting and teaching another's son.

glossary.en: ti bi ji ling - look at the wagtail
glossary.note: Ti is 'to look'; ji ling is the wagtail.
Tian is the same as 'ill'; yi an yi yu means facing the court and jail, to meet prison.

xiaowan.background: The Mao Preface says a grandee wrote it to mock King You; Zhu Xi said a grandee met a time of disorder and brothers warned one another to escape disaster. The last three lines were quoted by Zengzi on his deathbed in the Analects (Tai Bo) and became a motto of careful conduct. Some modern readers take the poem as an elder's warning to his descendants.

heming.summary: A poem of the Lesser Odes that teaches by images. A crane crying in the marsh, heard far over the wilds, shows a worthy man whose fame spreads though he hides; fish in the deeps or shallows show shifting hiding and showing. The close, 「它山之石，可以攻玉」 ("stones from another hill can polish jade"), says one can finish oneself by using others' strengths, and began a long line of later argument.
heming.translation:
The crane cries in the ninefold marsh, its voice is heard in the wilds.
The fish dive deep in the pool, or lie in the shallows.
How pleasant is that garden, with sandalwood planted, and fallen leaves beneath.
Stones from another hill can serve as whetstones.
The crane cries in the ninefold marsh, its voice is heard in the sky.
The fish lie in the shallows, or dive deep in the pool.
How pleasant is that garden, with sandalwood planted, and paper mulberry beneath.
Stones from another hill can polish jade.

glossary.note: A winding, remote marshland; gao is low ground by water.

glossary.en: sheng wen yu ye - its voice is heard in the wilds
glossary.note: The crane's call reaches the fields, meaning that a worthy man's fame spreads though he stays hidden.
A small islet in the water.

glossary.en: yuan you shu tan, qi xia wei tuo - sandalwood is planted, fallen leaves beneath (pronounced tuo)
glossary.note: Tan is a hard wood; tuo is fallen leaves.
A tree whose bark is used to make paper; its wood is poor, in contrast to sandalwood.

glossary.en: ta shan zhi shi, ke yi wei cuo - stones from another hill can be whetstones
glossary.note: Cuo is a whetstone.
To cut and polish jade; gong means to treat or process.

heming.background: The Mao Preface says it advises King Xuan, that is, urges him to seek worthy men; Zhu Xi said the poet used the wild crane to stand for a hermit sage. The line 「它山之石，可以攻玉」 became a well-known idiom meaning to learn from others' strengths and even from criticism so as to correct oneself.

wenwang.summary: The first poem of the Greater Odes, in the 'Odes' division, a hymn from early Zhou praising King Wen's achievements and warning later generations. It sings that Wen's virtue won the Mandate of Heaven and Zhou replaced Shang by Heaven's will, then warns the former Yin officials and Zhou's descendants to take Yin as a warning, cultivate virtue and fit the Mandate. It is a core text for the Zhou idea of Heaven's Mandate.
wenwang.translation:
King Wen is on high, and shines bright in Heaven.
Zhou is an old state, but its mandate is new.
How illustrious is Zhou; how timely the Lord's command.
King Wen goes up and down, at the Lord's side.
Tireless King Wen, his good name never fades.
Blessing was bestowed again and again on Zhou, on the descendants of King Wen.
King Wen's descendants, main line and branches, will last a hundred generations.
All the officers of Zhou are illustrious, generation after generation.
Illustrious through the generations, their counsel is careful and reverent.
How splendid are the many worthy men, born in this royal state.
The royal state was able to bring them forth, the pillars of Zhou.
Many and stately, the worthy men; through them King Wen is at peace.
Majestic King Wen - ah, how his reverent conduct shines, bright and unceasing.
Great is the mandate of Heaven, that has passed to the descendants of Shang.
The descendants of Shang number more than a hundred thousand.
Once the Lord on High gave his command, they submitted to Zhou.
They submit to Zhou; the mandate of Heaven is not constant.
The officers of Yin, handsome and quick, pour libations and assist in the Zhou capital.
In this service of libation they still wear the embroidered robe and the Yin cap.
You loyal ministers of the king, remember your ancestor.
Remember your ancestor, and cultivate his virtue.
Keep long in harmony with the mandate, and seek many blessings for yourselves.
Before Yin lost the multitude, it could stand as an equal to the Lord on High.
Take Yin as your mirror: the great mandate is not easily kept.
The mandate is not easily kept; do not let it end with you.
Make your good name shine, and ponder how Yin fell from Heaven's favour.
The work of high Heaven has no sound and no smell.
Take King Wen as your model, and the ten thousand states will trust you.

keyLines.en: Though Zhou is an old state, its mandate is new.
keyLines.note: Zhou is an ancient state, but the Mandate it received is fresh, showing that Zhou's replacing Shang followed Heaven's will.

keyLines.en: King Wen ascends and descends, at the side of the Lord on High.
keyLines.note: King Wen's spirit goes up and down between heaven and earth, always beside the Lord on High.

keyLines.en: How splendid are the many worthy men, born in this kingdom.
keyLines.note: The many fine scholars born in this realm are the basis of Zhou's rise.

keyLines.en: They submit to Zhou; the mandate of Heaven is not constant.
keyLines.note: The descendants of Shang have yielded to Zhou, showing that Heaven's Mandate does not stay with one house for ever.

keyLines.en: Do not forget your ancestors; cultivate their virtue.
keyLines.note: Do not forget your forebears; cultivate your own virtue.

keyLines.en: You should take Yin as a mirror; the great mandate is not easily kept.
keyLines.note: Take Yin as a lesson; the Mandate is not easy to keep.

keyLines.en: The work of Heaven has no sound and no smell.
keyLines.note: What Heaven does has no sound or smell, deep and beyond measure.

keyLines.en: Take King Wen as your model, and all states will trust you.
keyLines.note: If you model yourself on King Wen, all the states will come to trust you.

glossary.en: wu zhao yu tian - oh, he shines in Heaven
glossary.note: Wu is an exclamation; zhao is bright. It means that King Wen shines brightly in Heaven.

glossary.en: zhi jiang - to ascend and descend
glossary.note: To go up and down; the king's spirit moves between heaven and earth.
Diligent and unwearied.

glossary.en: ben zhi bai shi - main line and branches for a hundred generations
glossary.note: Ben is the direct line and zhi the collateral lines; it means descendants flourishing for generations.
A helping word, like wei.

glossary.en: guan jiang - to pour libation and assist
glossary.note: Guan is to pour wine on the ground in offering, jiang is to assist; the Yin officials helped at the rite in the Zhou capital.

glossary.en: fu xu - embroidered robe and Yin cap
glossary.note: Fu is a robe embroidered with axe patterns; xu is the ceremonial cap of the Yin people.

glossary.en: yi xing - to take as a model
glossary.note: To imitate and take as a pattern.

wenwang.background: The Mao Preface says King Wen received the Mandate and founded Zhou; Zhu Xi said the Duke of Zhou recalled King Wen's virtue to warn King Cheng. The ideas that 'Heaven's Mandate is not constant' and 'the mirror of Yin is not far off' were important reflections by early Zhou rulers on the rise and fall of Xia and Shang, and had a deep influence on later political thought.

mian.summary: A poem of the Greater Odes, an epic in which the Zhou people recall their ancestor Gugong Danfu moving to Mount Qi and building a home, and the rise of Zhou. Beginning with the unbroken melon vines, it tells of the move to Qi, divination, house-building and the palace, then the founding of the state's institutions and King Wen settling the dispute between Yu and Rui.
