It is the foundation epic of the Zhou people.
mian.translation:
Unbroken run the melon vines; when the people were first born,
it was from the Tu, the Ju and the Qi.
Gugong Danfu dug cave-homes and pits,
when there were yet no houses.
Gugong Danfu came at dawn galloping his horse,
along the western river banks to the foot of Mount Qi.
With Lady Jiang he came to look over the site.
The plain of Zhou was rich; even violets and bitter herbs were sweet as malt sugar.
There he began and planned; he cut marks in the tortoise shell.
It said: stay, the time is right; build houses here.
So they settled in peace, spread to left and right,
marked boundaries and drew fields, drained ditches and laid out furrows.
From west to east, all went about their tasks.
He summoned the Master of Works, he summoned the Master of Multitudes,
to raise the houses, with plumb-lines straight.
They bound the boards and loaded them, and raised the temple, orderly.
They scoop earth in, reng-reng, and pour it in the frames, hong-hong.
They pound it, deng-deng, and trim the bulges, ping-ping.
A hundred walls rise together; the great drum cannot out-beat them.
They set up the Outer Gate, tall and lofty.
They set up the Main Gate, stately and grand.
They set up the great altar of earth, from which armies march out.
So he did not erase their anger, but did not lose his good name either.
The oaks and thorn bushes were cleared; the roads opened.
The Hun barbarians fled, panting.
Yu and Rui submitted their dispute and made peace; King Wen stirred them to good.
I say, he had those who bring the distant close; I say, he had those who go before and behind.
I say, he had those who hurry to proclaim; I say, he had those who fend off insult.

glossary.en: gua die - melon and small melon
glossary.note: Die is a small melon; the unbroken vines stand for descendants who never fail.

glossary.en: Gugong Danfu - Gugong Danfu (pronounced dan fu)
glossary.note: The grandfather of King Wen, later honoured as Taiwang.

glossary.en: tao fu tao xue - dug dwellings and cave pits
glossary.note: Tao is to dig; fu xue is layers of cave dwellings, meaning the early cave homes.

glossary.en: Zhou yuan wu wu - the plain of Zhou was rich
glossary.note: Zhou yuan is the plain below Mount Qi; wu wu is rich and fertile soil.

glossary.en: yuan qi wo gui - to cut marks in my tortoise shell
glossary.note: Qi means to carve, to divine by carved shell.

glossary.en: suo ban yi zai - to bind the boards and load them
glossary.note: Suo is to bind; ban is the board used in pounding walls.

glossary.en: gao men, ying men - the Outer Gate, the Main Gate
glossary.note: The outer gate and main gate of an ancient palace.

glossary.en: Yu Rui zhi cheng - Yu and Rui settle their dispute
glossary.note: Yu and Rui quarrelled over land and asked King Wen to judge; zhi is to judge and cheng is a peaceful settlement.

mian.background: The Mao Preface says King Wen's rise came from Taiwang; Zhu Xi said the Duke of Zhou recalled how Taiwang moved to Qi and King Wen thereby raised Zhou. The move to Qi, the city and the altar, and the settlement of Yu and Rui are also recorded in the Records of the Grand Historian (Zhou Benji), making this an important source for early Zhou history.

shengmin.summary: A poem of the Greater Odes, a hymn sung at the sacrifice to the ancestor Hou Ji. It tells how Hou Ji's mother Jiang Yuan conceived him by treading on the Lord on High's footprint, how he was abandoned yet protected by Heaven, farmed from childhood, grew the hundred grains as an adult, and began the sacrifices. It is the origin myth of the Zhou people and a record of early farming civilisation.
shengmin.translation:
In the beginning, who bore the people? It was Jiang Yuan.
How did she bear them? She made pure offerings and sacrifices, that she might no longer be childless.
She trod on the Lord's footprint, in the big toe, and was moved; she was blessed, and she rested.
Then she conceived, then she kept herself in reverent seclusion; then she bore him, then she raised him. This was Hou Ji.
When her months were full, the first birth came as easily as a lamb's.
No tearing, no splitting, no trouble, no harm.
So that his divine power should shine out, the Lord on High was at ease with her offerings, and she bore her son just so.
He was set down in a narrow lane, but cattle and sheep sheltered and nursed him.
He was set down in the wide wood, but woodcutters came to the wood.
He was set down on cold ice, and birds covered him with their wings.
When the birds flew away, Hou Ji cried out.
Long and loud was his cry, and it filled the road.
Soon he crawled, then he could stand tall and bright, and seek his own food.
He planted large beans, and the beans grew in waving banners; his rows of grain were heavy with ears.
Hemp and wheat grew thick, and melons and gourds hung heavy.
Hou Ji's farming had a way of helping the land:
he cleared away the rank grass and sowed the fine yellow seed.
It sprouted and swelled, it grew thick and tall, it shot up and flowered, it was firm and fine, it bore full ears and heavy grain.
Then he was given a house and home at Tai.
Heaven sent down fine seed: black millet, double-grain black millet, red sorghum, white sorghum.
Black millet and double-grain millet were planted far and wide, harvested and stacked in heaps.
Red and white sorghum were planted far and wide, carried on shoulder and on back.
They brought them home, to begin the sacrifices.
And how are our sacrifices done? Some pound the grain, some scoop it out, some winnow, some tread it.
It is rinsed, sou-sou, and steamed, fu-fu.
Then we plan and ponder: we take southernwood and burn it with fat, we take a ram for the road sacrifice,
we roast it and we grill it, to bring in the coming year.
We heap the food in the wooden stands and in the earthenware dishes.
As the fragrance begins to rise, the Lord on High is pleased and accepts it.
How truly timely is the scent! Hou Ji began the sacrifice, hoping to be free of fault and regret, and it has lasted to this day.

keyLines.en: When the people were first born, it was Jiang Yuan.
keyLines.note: The first person to bear the Zhou people was Jiang Yuan.

keyLines.en: She trod on the Lord's footprint, felt moved, and was blessed and rested.
keyLines.note: She stepped on the Lord on High's footprint, felt something stir, and so conceived.

keyLines.line: 誕寘之隘巷，牛羊腓字之
keyLines.en: He was set down in a narrow lane, but cattle and sheep sheltered and nursed him.
keyLines.note: The child was thrown in a narrow lane, yet cattle and sheep shielded and fed him.

keyLines.en: He was set down on cold ice, and birds covered him with their wings.
keyLines.note: He was laid on ice, and birds covered him with their wings.

keyLines.en: He was bright and upright, and could seek his own food.
keyLines.note: As a small child he was wise and stood tall, and could find his own food.

keyLines.line: 誕降嘉種，維秬維秠，維穈維芑
keyLines.en: Heaven sent down fine seed: black millet, double-grain millet, red sorghum, white sorghum.
keyLines.note: Heaven sent good seeds: black millet, a black millet with two grains to a husk, red sorghum and white sorghum.

keyLines.line: 后稷肇祀，庶無罪悔，以迄于今
keyLines.en: Hou Ji began the sacrifice, hoping for no fault or regret, down to this day.
keyLines.note: Hou Ji began the rites, hoping to be free from fault and regret, and they continue to this day.

glossary.note: Hou Ji's mother, said to be the chief consort of Emperor Ku.

glossary.en: ke yin ke si - she made pure offerings and sacrifices
glossary.note: Yin is a clean sacrifice and si is a sacrifice; she prayed devoutly for a child.

glossary.en: lu Di wu min xin - she trod on the Lord's footprint and felt moved
glossary.note: She stepped on the footprint of the Lord on High (at the heel or big toe), was moved and glad, and is said to have conceived.

glossary.en: xian sheng ru da - the first birth as easy as a lamb's
glossary.note: Her first labour was easy, like a lamb being born; da is a lamb.

glossary.en: fei zi - to shelter and nurse
glossary.note: Fei is to protect; zi is to feed.
Soybeans.

glossary.en: ju, pi, mi, qi - four grains
glossary.note: Ju is black millet; pi is black millet with two kernels to a husk; mi is red sorghum; qi is white sorghum.

glossary.en: ba - to sacrifice to the road god (pronounced ba)
glossary.note: A sacrifice to the god of the road; here a ram is taken for it.

shengmin.background: The Mao Preface says it honours the ancestor, that is, the sacrifice to Hou Ji as equal to Heaven; Zhu Xi said the Zhou people traced Hou Ji's birth to use in the suburban sacrifice. The poem keeps a myth of miraculous birth: Jiang Yuan treading on the Lord's footprint and giving birth to Hou Ji, which shows how early peoples traced their ancestors. Hou Ji was later honoured as the god of farming.

qingmiao.summary: The first poem of the Hymns of Zhou, in the 'Hymns' division, sung by the Zhou royal house at the sacrifice to King Wen. It shows the solemn, quiet temple, the grave assistants, many worthy men holding to King Wen's virtue, and people hurrying about the temple. The language is spare and stately.
qingmiao.translation:
O solemn pure temple, reverent and harmonious the illustrious helpers.
Many worthy men, holding to King Wen's virtue.
Answering him who is in Heaven, they hurry to and fro in the temple.
How bright, how honoured - never wearied of by men.

glossary.note: Wu is an exclamation; mu is grave and solemn.
A quiet, solemn ancestral temple, meaning the temple where King Wen is honoured.

glossary.en: su yong xian xiang - reverent, harmonious, illustrious helpers
glossary.note: Su is respectful, yong is harmonious; xian xiang are the ministers and lords who assist at the rite.

glossary.en: ji ji duo shi - many worthy men in good order
glossary.note: A large and orderly body of fine scholars.

glossary.en: bing wen zhi de - to hold to King Wen's virtue
glossary.note: To keep and carry on King Wen's virtue.

glossary.en: dui yue zai tian - answering him in Heaven
glossary.note: Dui is to reply and yue to praise; zai tian is King Wen, who is in Heaven.

glossary.en: jun ben zou - to hurry about
glossary.note: To run quickly, meaning the bustle of assisting at the rite.
Yi is the same as a word for 'to be tired of'.

qingmiao.background: The Mao Preface says it is for sacrificing to King Wen: the Duke of Zhou finished the city of Luoyi, received the lords at court and led them in the rite; Zhu Xi said the same. The Hymns of Zhou are mostly sacrificial songs; 'Pure Temple' stands first of the 'Hymns' and is short in form, a song sung during the rite itself.
